title: THE STARRY NIGHT
transcript: Alright, so find the big white star. Left of the middle, just to the right of that dark tree. The one with all that light around it. That’s the one he wrote his brother Theo about. You know this guy. Vincent van Gogh. More than two thousand paintings and drawings in about ten years. Sells hardly anything. Sales have… you know… picked up. Anyway, when he paints this, he’s a patient in an asylum in the south of France. Checked himself in. Iron bars on his bedroom window. One morning, way before sunrise, he looks out, and there’s this light. He writes to Theo about that big morning star. That’s actually Venus. The planet. But that town? He couldn’t see it from there. He put it in. He pulls that dark tree way closer than it really was. And up in the sky, he changes the shapes and turns up the glow. Back in Arles, he tells Theo the stars are like the black dots on a map. Why should the lights up there be any harder to get to? You take the train to the next town over. You take death to go to a star… Dying of old age? That’s walking. So… he paints it in a spare room. A night sky, painted during the day. Short strokes, one after another, looping around that big swirl. Around every star, rings of white and yellow, pushed out and out. So go back to that white light. The one that looked very big. That November, he writes to a painter friend. Says he’s made the stars too big again. He calls it… another failure.

title: SELF PORTRAIT IN A STRAW HAT
transcript: Alright, let’s start with the straw hat. Dark band. Tipped back a little. Big dark beard under it. Eyes off to the side. That’s Paul Cézanne. Picasso and Matisse both supposedly called him “the father of us all.” So, speaking of fathers… it’s 1878, he’s thirty-nine, and he’s still on an allowance from his. Dad’s a banker. His name’s literally on a bank in the south of France. But… Paul has this small secret… just a… another family. With a lady named Hortense, and a son. Also Paul. Let’s call him little Paul. He’s six. They’re in Marseille. He’s been keeping that little secret from Dad. Then a collector friend writes to Cézanne. Mentions “Madame Cézanne and little Paul.” His father opens the letter first. So… now Dad knows. And suddenly the money gets tight. Cézanne now only gets a hundred francs a month. That’s half what his father had promised. So he hits up his old school friend, the writer Émile Zola. Sixty francs a month, straight to Hortense. He calls it his “monthly prayer.” Then unexpectedly in September, Dad just hands over three hundred francs. Paul writes Zola, “Unheard of.” Then adds, he thinks Dad’s got a crush on the maid. Anyway, come back to the painting. Those big swirls behind his head. It’s wallpaper. The same pattern appears behind his mother and sister in a painting from about eight years earlier. At the family house. So that’s probably where he’s painted this. Under Dad’s roof. Still needing Dad’s money. Trying to keep his own family out of the conversation. And one last thing about Dad. Before the bank, he made hats. Had a shop on the main street in Aix. So… look at what his son put on.

title: MILK CAN AND APPLES
transcript: So... something's wrong with this table. Take a second. Try to find it. There it is. The tilt. The whole top sorta tips up toward you, steep enough that the apples should be in your lap by now. The milk can just stands there like the table is level. Does that look level to you? This is Cézanne. Milk Can and Apples. Around 1880. Now try to figure out the spot you're seeing it from. The tabletop, you're looking down on from up high. But the apples, you're seeing almost from the side, like you pulled up a chair. And that front edge runs flat across the bottom. The angles don't quite agree. And perspective had rules... Ya know... Centuries of them. Cézanne said he copies nature "while interpreting it." He died in 1906. A year later, Paris put on a big show of his work. A young painter named Georges Braque had already been painting at L'Estaque, near Marseille. Cézanne's old territory. Which is why he picked it. The next summer, Braque goes back. Paints houses packed together, walls and roofs pressed into geometric blocks. And the walls don't agree on an angle either. Sorta what this table does. Then he sends those landscapes to a Paris exhibition. The Salon d'Automne. The jury turns them down. That guy Matisse is on the jury. So a dealer shows them instead. And then a critic complains that Braque has reduced everything to cubes. Houses, landscape, the lot. The insult sticks. Cubism. Now look back at the table. Years later, Braque explained what bothered him about the old perspective. It starts from one spot, he said. And never leaves it.

title: THE BATHER
transcript: Okay, so, here's a Cézanne thing nobody really tells you. When he was a kid, somebody kicked him on a staircase, and he just... never got over it. Couldn't be touched after that. Whole life. Flinched at a handshake. So guess what he spends the next forty years painting. Naked people. Bodies, everywhere. The one guy who can't stand to be touched, totally obsessed with the one thing that's all about touching. Anyway. Watch what he does with that. This guy here. Alone, hand on his hip, head down, standing in water that's barely even there. And there's no model in the room, by the way. He's working off a photograph, propped up across the studio. Nice and far. Nothing breathing on him. And he paints this body the exact same way he'd paint an apple. Same strokes on the skin as on the sky. Not flattering it, not warming it up. Just... building it. Like a thing. And honestly, that's about where the whole twentieth century cracks open. Because once a body is just shapes that have to hold together, you're maybe three steps from Cubism. From Picasso. From everything coming next. Look at him. He's stiff, he's awkward, he won't quite meet your eye, and that's the whole life of it. A real person, caught not performing. The guy who couldn't stand to be touched, painting the one person in here you kind of want to reach out to. And the photograph is in this building too. Somebody donated it. Nobody knows who took it, or who the kid was. Cézanne kept him across the studio his whole life. Now they're in the same collection.

title: EVENING, HONFLEUR
transcript: Alright, so, there are at least twenty-five colors in this thing. But… it looks like a handful. Gray. Green. A little pink. Go ahead. Try to find… twenty. Now get up close. It’s just dots. Thousands of them, sitting side by side. That’s where the rest are hiding. Those gray clouds, up close, are blue dots and orange dots. Your eye made the gray. The green water’s got yellow in it. Even the pink beach is full of blue. Okay, now back up a bit… There it is. One little box of evening. So, Seurat came to Honfleur, on the coast of Normandy. Said he wanted to “wash the light of the studio” out of his eyes. He’d been reading about optics. How our eyes see color. So he puts the colors next to each other in little dots. Lets the person looking do the mixing. He paints the dots. You put the picture together. And from here, it shimmers. So… Seurat’s only twenty-six when he paints this. The dot thing gets a name. Pointillism. Which makes sense… it’s just dots. His friend Signac picks it up. Then a whole crowd of painters after him. Seurat doesn’t get to see where it goes. A few years after this, he’s dead. At only thirty-one. Now the frame. He painted that too. Added it later. Same stuff, but easier to pick out here. Up in the top right, the dots get a little lighter. Like the sunset keeps going. Right out of the box.

title: BOY IN A RED VEST
transcript: Look at this kid. He's done. Checked out. Not posing, not performing, just... enduring. His name was Michelangelo di Rosa, a professional model, whose whole job was to sit still for hours while Cézanne stared at him like a math problem. And he painted him four times. Same kid, same red vest, same boredom. Now... a portrait is supposed to be about the person. The charm, the spark, the look that says here I am. Cézanne wants none of it. A kid working to look good gives you a nice portrait. A kid who's completely given up gives you something way better. Just a person, holding still long enough to turn into pure paint. So look what he does. That vest isn't even really red. The whole boy is built out of little patches of color, blue, green, grey, knots of violet, each one testing whether it can hold next to the one beside it. He's not painting a boy. He's solving a boy. Like a still life that happens to have a pulse. Drain all the personality out, treat him like furniture, and that should be a dead end. It isn't. That slumped, bored, get-me-out-of-here teenager turns out to be the realest person in the room. And get this. Before any museum owned it, somebody else did. None other than Claude Monet. He called it the best picture he owned. Not one of his own works. This one.

title: THE OLIVE TREES
transcript: Alright, so… look at that dark blue ridge, left of the middle. Two holes in it. Like somebody punched straight through the rock. Keep those in mind. So, Van Gogh’s living at the asylum in the south of France. When he’s well enough, he goes out to paint the olive trees. He’s had his eye on them for a while. Before he even gets there, he’s telling his brother they remind him of the old willows in Dutch fields. Too beautiful to dare paint. Then… he dares. And they turn out to be a real pain. The leaves keep changing color on him. Silver, sometimes blue, sometimes greenish. Really hard, he admits. But… he’s into it. Look how the curves in the ground run up through the trunks and into the leaves. That famous one, with all those swirls up in the night sky, is from around this time, too. Here, he’s got that same energy running through the dirt. He wants the silver to be his, the way yellow was with the sunflowers. Plus, he figures, hardly anybody paints olive trees. So, he just keeps going back. By the end of the year, he’s made about fifteen of these olive paintings. This is one of the first. Anyway, back to those holes. People have read his mental illness into them. Figured he must have invented something that strange. But that’s a real rock outside Saint-Rémy. Les Deux Trous. The Two Holes. You can walk up there and see them.

title: OPUS 217. AGAINST THE ENAMEL OF A BACKGROUND RHYTHMIC WITH BEATS AND ANGLES, TONES, AND TINTS, PORTRAIT OF M. FÉLIX FÉNÉON IN 1890
transcript: Okay. See the elegant man in profile, holding out a little flower? A few years after this, he plants a bomb in a Paris restaurant. That's Félix Fénéon. By day, a chief clerk at the French War Ministry. Also an anarchist. Also, somehow, the most important art critic in Paris. He coins the word Neo-Impressionism. He champions Seurat and Signac when everyone else thinks the whole little-dots business is a headache. You have to admit, the man has range. It's 1894. A bomb goes off at a restaurant called Foyot. The police search his office at the War Ministry and, get this, find detonators in his desk. So they put him on trial with a roomful of other anarchists. And he is delightful about it. The judge says he'd been spotted talking to a known anarchist behind a gas lamp. And Fénéon goes, tell me, your honor, which side of a gas lamp is its behind? The jury loves him. Acquitted. Of course. And then he goes right back to writing about painting. That is who Signac is painting. And look how he does it. Fénéon in strict profile, top hat and cane in one hand, the flower held out in the other, not even looking at it. While behind him the entire universe detonates. Spirals, stars, rainbow bands, a pinwheel of color spinning straight out of his fingertips. The bomber, standing there, not flinching, while the whole world goes off behind him. And that universe he's so calm in front of? Signac didn't invent it. He copied it off a Japanese print he owned, a pattern from a kimono. The wildest thing in the painting is wallpaper.

title: THE SLEEPING GYPSY
transcript: So this is the guy Picasso threw a banquet for. We’ll get there. Look at the lion first. He’s standing over a sleeping woman in the middle of a desert. And he’s not attacking her. He’s sniffing her. She’s out cold. Mandolin by her hand, a jug of water, a walking stick. Not a drop of blood. Henri Rousseau. Self-taught. For twenty-two years, he collects taxes on goods coming into Paris. So people start calling him Le Douanier. The customs officer. It sticks. The guy never saw a desert. He studies animals in Paris, works from pictures. Then puts them somewhere he’s never been. And he’s serious about this. Two years before he paints it, he writes his own little biography. Says he’s on his way to becoming one of the best realist painters around. Realist. Seriously… Look at that moon. The year after he paints this, he writes to the mayor of Laval, his hometown, and offers them the painting. Calls it a souvenir from one of the town’s children. And he explains what’s happening. A lion wanders over, picks up the woman’s scent, and doesn’t eat her. He’s asking about two thousand francs. Laval says no. And the painting drops out of sight. Ten years later, Picasso throws him that banquet. There’s a banner: Honor to Rousseau. Rousseau takes out his violin and plays a waltz he wrote himself. And, the story goes, tells Picasso they’re the two greatest painters of their time. You in the Egyptian style. Me in the modern. By every account, he meant it. Meanwhile, nobody knows where this thing is. It turns up in 1924, at a charcoal dealer’s in Paris. Rousseau’s been dead fourteen years. In 1939, it gets here. The next year, MoMA’s director calls it one of the great masterpieces of modern times. Laval could’ve had it for about two thousand francs. So look at the lion one more time. He seems to be looking past her. Like he forgot why he walked over.

title: PINES AND ROCKS (FONTAINEBLEAU?)
transcript: The title of this one is Pines and Rocks. Then, in parentheses, Fontainebleau… question mark. So… what’s up with the question mark? Fontainebleau’s an actual forest near Paris. But for years, people thought this was Provence. Cézanne’s home turf. Other end of the country. Look at those rusty red pines. Grey rocks going pink. Blue poking through the branches. Gorgeous. But good luck getting an address out of it. Look at the pale gaps between the brushstrokes. That’s just bare canvas. And where there is paint, it’s thin. Almost like watercolor. That thin paint, by the way, is what moved the date back. They had it down as one of his last. About seven years earlier, when he’s spending time near Paris. So… the question mark stays. But those bare patches? Depends who you ask. A couple of years before he painted this, Cézanne finally gets his own show. He’s fifty-six. His old friend Pissarro goes to see it and writes his son afterward. Says some of the still lifes are perfect. But there are others that look like they aren’t even finished yet, and he likes those even better. And Cézanne himself? He’s not so sure. Near the end of his life, he writes a younger painter about the color, the light. Those little places where one thing meets another. He can’t quite get it all down. Can’t cover the whole canvas. The picture stays incomplete. Now look back at those gaps. He was already leaving them here. Years before he tried to explain them.

title: LE VOYAGE DANS LA LUNE
transcript: So… a bunch of astronomers climb into a giant bullet and get fired out of a cannon. They land on the moon. Have a nap. Start hitting the locals with umbrellas. Get captured. Kill the king. Then escape by tipping their capsule off the edge of the moon. Fall back to Earth. Into the ocean. This is A Trip to the Moon. MoMA calls it the first science-fiction film. And the guy who made it? A magician named Georges Méliès. So, one day, Georges goes to see the Lumières’ new machine. The way he tells it, there’s a photograph of a town square up on the screen. Then, unexpectedly, a horse in the photograph starts moving. By the end, he’s offering ten thousand francs for the machine. They won’t sell. So… he builds a glass studio in his garden. Basically a greenhouse with a stage in it. And he starts doing his magic on film. Anyway, watch for the moon coming toward you. That’s actually a man sitting in a chair, covered up to the neck in black velvet. They’re pulling him toward the camera. And those moon creatures are acrobats from the Folies Bergère. One of them gets whacked with an umbrella. Puff of smoke. Gone. Really, they just stop the camera and let the acrobat walk out of the shot. Start filming again, join the two bits of film together, and he’s vanished. And that’s a big reason they call him the father of special effects. Now, the guy with the big white beard, running the whole expedition? That’s Méliès. And the moon? The face in the velvet, with a capsule in its eye? That’s him too.

title: LANDSCAPE AT COLLIOURE
transcript: Ah, Matisse! You can feel the sun coming off this before you can tell what it is. There's a hillside in there. We're in Collioure, a little fishing town near the Spanish border. It's the summer of 1905. Matisse is down there painting with his friend André Derain. He's thirty-five. Fifteen years earlier, he was a law clerk. Then appendicitis put him in bed, and his mother brought him a box of paints. And well... ya know... gave up law. And here he is, making the ground pink. The tree trunks go red. Between the dabs, you can see the raw canvas. He puts paint straight onto it, then leaves a lot of it showing. You might think he's going to come back and fill it in. But he isn't. This is finished. The trees are the wrong color. But the heat feels right. That little trade helps change modern painting. Then comes Paris. That fall, Matisse and the others show their new paintings in a big exhibition. In the middle of their room, somebody's put a tidy little bust of a child. A critic looks at the bust. Looks around at the paintings. Then writes: "Donatello among the wild beasts." Donatello didn't make the bust. The bust just gets to be Donatello. Matisse and his friends get to be animals. Fauves. Wild beasts. The name sticks. Fauvism. You can put it in a textbook now. Years later, Matisse's son-in-law said Matisse still had no idea what Fauvism meant.

title: BOY LEADING A HORSE
transcript: A naked kid, walking a horse. That's the whole picture. Now look at his right hand. Closed in a fist at the horse's chest. Look for what's in it. Nothin'. No rope, no bridle, no halter. Check the whole horse. Not one piece of leather on the animal. It follows him anyway. People love that part. Sure. It's the wrong mystery. The real one is the land. No road. No water. No buildings, trees, or people. Pink dirt, low hills, a sky doing the bare minimum. An old MoMA catalogue calls it "a kind of nonenvironment." Fancy way of saying there's nothing out there. Paris, winter into 1906. Picasso is planning something huge. A watering place. Horses drinking, riders, boys. And through the middle, this kid leading a horse to the water. He works it out over and over. Gouache, watercolor, a drawing, a little drypoint. Then he drops it. The big picture never gets made. But this kid he keeps. Cuts him out of the crowd and gives him a canvas over seven feet tall. A real face. Calm. Classical. Clock that face. The rest of this room is what happens to it. Everything else from the plan is gone. The riders. The boys. Even the water. Maybe that's why the place reads like nowhere. You're looking at the middle of a picture that doesn't exist. One more thing. The plan survived. MoMA owns the drypoint. Barely bigger than a postcard. Every rider, every horse, this same boy. The whole plan fits in your hand. The boy Picasso kept needed seven feet.

title: NUDE WITH JOINED HANDS
transcript: Picasso took his girlfriend Fernande and gave her a face about two thousand years old. Look at her. The body's still a real person. Pink skin. Real weight. Bent knee. Hands clasped together. Then the face. Flat. Almond eyes. Little shut mouth. Like somebody carved it. And Fernande's not the first woman this happened to. All that winter, Gertrude Stein had been sitting for Picasso. Eighty or ninety times, according to Stein. And he could not get her face right. Then one day, he paints the whole head out. "I can't see you any more when I look." He says. Right around then, Picasso sees ancient Iberian sculpture at the Louvre. Faces more than two thousand years old. Flat. Almond eyes. Small mouths. Then he and Fernande head up to Gósol in the Pyrenees. And he starts this painting. Look at the face again. There they are. By the end of the summer, Picasso's back in Paris. He finishes Stein's portrait without another sitting. Same hard, simplified face. People tell him it doesn't look like her. Picasso says, "She will." That portrait's at the Met, right across town. And Gertrude Stein bought this painting too. She kept it for the rest of her life. Thirty-three years. So after all that trouble over her own face, she spent thirty-three years with this one.

title: TWO NUDES
transcript: Picasso knows exactly how to make a body look graceful. And then he makes this. Two naked women packed into a space that feels about a foot too small. Elbows out. Shoulders up. They're not hugging. They look like two people who've been stuck in the same room way too long. And the whole thing feels heavy. Awkward. Almost clumsy. Like Picasso forgot how to be Picasso. But, he didn't. He'd just come back from Gósol, this little village up in the Pyrenees, and something had changed up there. The bodies got bigger. Simpler. More stone than person. Then back in Paris, he pushes it even further. Terracotta skin. Huge limbs. Those heavy faces. He'd been looking at Iberian sculpture. And you can feel it here. No elegance. No showing off. Just weight. Even the two women barely fit together. Like, can you scoot over? Nope. Now look at the woman on the left. She's pulling open a curtain. And she's looking right at you. Get a good look at her face. Then go find Les Demoiselles d'Avignon. It's hanging in this same gallery, painted a few months later. Look at the woman on the far left. Same curtain. Same chiseled nose. Same dark, hollow eyes. Picasso's not at Les Demoiselles yet. But she's already here.

title: WOMAN PLAITING HER HAIR
transcript: A woman, fixing her hair. Most ordinary thing in the world. So why does she look like she was built for a temple? Picasso had spent that whole summer in the Spanish Pyrenees, in a village called Gósol. He gets back to Paris in August. And then he paints this. Blank, ancient-looking face. Heavy body. Looks dug up, not painted. And actually, Picasso wasn't done with the idea. That same August, he makes another woman doing her hair. Out of clay this time. He fires her in a kiln in the kitchen of a potter friend up in Montmartre. A Basque guy named Paco Durrio, who'd been badgering him for ages to try clay. First thing he ever made in clay. So this little everyday thing, fixing your hair, keeps coming out of his hands like some ancient ritual. And that's the weird part. He's not painting a queen. She's not doing anything heroic. She's just getting ready. And somehow the moment gets all this weight. Now jump thirty-four years. Picasso paints another woman doing her hair. Same basic gesture. Completely different woman. And this time? It looks like the end of the world.

title: LES DEMOISELLES D'AVIGNON
transcript: So. This painting has a seam. Look at the faces on the left. Calm. Almost ancient. The two in the middle especially. Arms up, eyes staring out like statues. Now look at the two on the right. Masks. Blunt planes. Slashes across the faces. They barely look like they belong in the same painting. And, in a way, they don't. Picasso worked on this thing for months. The faces on the left grew out of the Iberian sculpture he'd been looking at all year. Then, midway through the painting, he goes to the Trocadéro. The old ethnographic museum in Paris. African and Oceanic masks. Wooden figures. Stuff he'd never seen like this before. He comes back to the canvas and those two faces on the right change completely. Not a perfect before-and-after. But pretty close. You can almost watch the painting change its mind. Look at the woman crouching in the bottom corner. Her body twists one way. Her face snaps straight at you. She's on the after side of the seam. And when Picasso's friends saw the finished painting, basically nobody knew what to do with it. Matisse thought it was an outrage. Derain supposedly said Picasso would end up hanged behind it. Braque hated it too. Then Braque came back. And within a year, he and Picasso were working side by side on what became Cubism. Picasso didn't show this painting publicly for almost nine years. But years later, he explained what had happened to him at the Trocadéro. Those masks didn't feel like art to him. They felt like protection. Weapons against things you were afraid of. And suddenly this whole painting made sense to him that way. He called it his first exorcism.

title: THE TEN LARGEST, NO. 7, ADULTHOOD
transcript: Okay. So this thing is over ten feet tall. She painted it in four days, lying on the floor, in 1907. That's before Kandinsky. Before Mondrian. Before anybody had decided you were even allowed to do this. And that's the whole thing. Nobody had done it yet. There's nothing to copy. She's not taking a tree and boiling it down to a shape. She's painting something that doesn't have a picture. Look at it. Roman numerals. Dashed lines, like a diagram. Looping letters down the side, an alphabet she made up and never bothered to translate. Pods, seeds, cells splitting in two. It's not a picture of anything. It's a map of something only she could see. This one's number seven. Adulthood. One of ten, the whole arc of a life, childhood to old age. The big yellow shapes, pinched in the middle, numbered one, two, three. Stages inside a stage. And here's the part nobody can quite handle. She's taking dictation. From spirits. She called them the High Masters, and they told her what to paint. Four days a canvas, then the next one. And no, that's not a figure of speech. She meant it, literally, spirits and all. Then you look at the wall, and if you ask me, the spirits had taste. Whatever was happening in that room, it worked. And she knew nobody was ready. Rudolf Steiner, the great spiritualist of the day, the one man who should have gotten it, stands in her doorway, looks at all of it, and tells her to wait. Fifty years, he says. He was being optimistic. So she makes it a rule, puts it in her will. Nobody sees these until she's been gone twenty years. And while she waits underground, Kandinsky walks off with the title. Father of abstraction. Not around to give it back. Oh, and she painted it for a temple. One that didn't exist. A spiral building, she said. Which sounds like more spirit talk, except they went and built it. It's the Guggenheim. A spiral she never walked into, full of paintings she never showed a soul.

title: SELF-PORTRAIT WITH TWO FLOWERS IN HER RAISED LEFT HAND
transcript: She's looking right at you. Not posing, just looking back. Like she's the one sizing you up. And in 1907, that's a radical thing to be doing. For five hundred years, women in paintings are there to get looked at. They're the model, never the one holding the brush. Paula Modersohn-Becker wasn't having it. A year or so before this, she'd painted herself nude. Just about the first woman anyone can name who'd tried it. So now she's both at once. The one holding the brush, and the one everybody's looking at. And she just... did it. Didn't ask. Here, she's covered up. Just her face, and two flowers held up in one hand, a red one and a pink one. But look at that face. Rough, thick, kind of built up in ridges, the cheeks too pink. It doesn't look like a normal portrait. It looks carved. Permanent. Like something dug up. And that's no accident. She'd been over at the Louvre, studying the Egyptian mummy portraits. The faces they laid over the dead, made to keep looking at the living long after the person's gone. That's the face she gives herself. One meant to outlast her. A few months later, she has a daughter. Eighteen days after the birth, she stands up for the first time, and a blood clot kills her. Thirty-one years old. More than seven hundred paintings, and she was barely getting started. They say she had time for one last word. Schade. What a pity. She had no idea any of that was coming. She just stood here and gave herself a face built to be remembered. Not a woman to be looked at. A woman doing the looking. Still holding up those two flowers. And here you are. The whoever comes next.

title: MUSIC (SKETCH)
transcript: Only one of these four people is actually making music. The guy with the violin. The two in the middle are dancing, all wrapped around each other. And the man down on the right is sitting this one out. Head in his hand. Listening. Nobody's looking at anybody. Matisse actually played the violin himself. Years later, his wife asked why he practiced so much. He told her he was afraid of going blind. If he couldn't paint anymore, he could still play. So. Backup plan. Now. This is called Music (Sketch). Look at those black lines. That's charcoal. He's drawing and painting on the same canvas, and he lets you see both. Finished enough to put in a big Paris show, though. He hangs it there in 1907. Gertrude Stein and her brother Leo buy it. Which leaves a question. A sketch for what? Because the big paintings haven't even been ordered yet. That happens two years later. A rich Russian guy wants two enormous paintings for his house in Moscow. One is Music. The other is Dance. In this little one, they're still all together. The violinist. The listener. The dancers. In the big Music, the violinist stays. So does the listener. The dancers... ya know, get their own wall.

title: DANCE (I)
transcript: You know this Matisse. Five pink naked people dancing on a hill. This is the first version. Technically, it's a sketch. Eight and a half feet tall. Nearly thirteen feet wide. Look at the dancer stretched across the bottom. One leg thrown back. Her whole body reaching toward the woman on the left. Their hands don't quite touch. That's not much of a grip. She's gotta keep moving. Blue sky. Green hill. Five bodies. Hardly a face between them. Nobody had really stripped a painting down this far before. Matisse figured the camera could handle the details now. Painting could go straight for the feeling. He'd watched fishermen do a ring dance on a beach near Spain. Here, the fishermen are gone. So are the beach and the clothes. He painted this in less than a week. A collector from Moscow saw it. Sergei Shchukin. At the end of March, he wrote Matisse that he was ready to "brave our bourgeois opinion" and hang nudes on his staircase. Meaning: fancy people would come over, see five naked dancers on the stairs, and have something to say. He was going to hang them there anyway. So Matisse painted another version. This time the dancers were red. Then the finished paintings went on show in Paris. The critics laid into them. And Shchukin backed out. So much for brave. Then, on the way home, he changed his mind again. The red dancers went to Moscow. They got their staircase. This pink one? Less than a week to paint. It took twenty-seven years for Matisse to let it go.

title: THE DREAM
transcript: Nobody could ever explain the couch. A naked woman, on a red velvet couch. The fancy kind, straight out of a Paris parlor. Sitting in the middle of a jungle. Not near one. In it. Vines, lotus flowers, an elephant in the leaves, a snake. A full moon up top, and two lions down below, staring straight out at you. And off in the dark, a little figure playing a flute. The whole thing is so green it's almost loud. People kept asking Rousseau about it. Bothered him enough that he wrote a poem to go with the painting. The gist: Yadwigha, fast asleep, deep in a beautiful dream, hears a snake charmer's pipe drifting in, and floats off into it. So the couch isn't in the jungle. She's dreaming the jungle. We're inside her sleep. So. Who's Yadwigha? A woman he loved, long, long ago. A Polish girl, from back when he was young. Gone, by the time he painted this. Sit with that. An old man, painting her young again. Naked, and somehow not in danger. And he builds her a whole paradise to do it in. Leaf by leaf, fifty shades of green, just so she'd have somewhere impossible to sleep. And this is the last thing he ever painted. He finished it, and a few months later, he was gone. So that's where his mind went, right at the end. Not home. Here. To her.

title: GIRL WITH A MANDOLIN (FANNY TELLIER)
transcript: Good news. This is the one you can actually see. Start with her head. Tipped down, off to one side, like she's watching her own fingers. Hair up in a bun. Below that, an actual mandolin. The round body, the dark sound hole, the neck climbing up to the right with her fingers on it. In this room, that's practically a photograph. The woman had a name. Fanny Tellier. Posing was her job. She'd sat for some of Picasso's friends, and she offered to sit for him. Then the sittings just kept going. Whatever she signed up for, it wasn't this. So Fanny says she's sick. Then she stops coming altogether. And Picasso stops. You can see that too. Some parts he took all the way. Look at the breast. Round, shaded, downright classical. Other parts get one thin wash of gray and then nothing. The painting quit when she did. And past the name, the record on Fanny is nearly empty. For decades, Picasso didn't even say who she was. Now the strange part. The autumn before, Paris put on a show of Corot. Gentle old landscape painter. Dead before either of them was born. But these were the ones he'd kept back. Figures. Quiet women sitting in studios, holding mandolins more than playing them. Twenty-four of them. Picasso walked through the show with Braque, the guy he was inventing all this with. And within a year, both of them had painted a woman with a mandolin. Braque's is in Madrid. This is Picasso's. The most radical painter in Europe, covering a dead man's tune. Maybe that's what the instrument is doing here. Give somebody a mandolin, and suddenly she can sit there like a pitcher on a table. Years later, somebody called it unfinished. He just shrugged, and said: "I really don't see what I could have added."

title: MAIASTRA
transcript: Alright, so a guy leaves Bucharest for Paris on foot. We’re talking about fifteen hundred miles. Walking, sleeping outside the whole thing. Stops in Munich to cut stone for a while. Near the end, he catches a train. Nobody can agree how long it took. Let’s just call it a year. The story goes he gets off the train on the fourteenth of July, which is Bastille Day. He liked to say France met him with a brass band and a military salute. His name is Constantin Brancusi. Peasant kid from the Carpathians. Been carving wood since he was little. He’ll become one of the most important sculptors of the century. But right now he just smells like the road. Three years later, he lands the job. Assistant to Rodin. Ya know, just the most famous sculptor alive. Then he quits after a few weeks. “Nothing grows under the shadow of big trees,” he says. Alright, so what does this guy make, now that he’s out from under the tree? The Măiastră. A bird with golden feathers from Romanian bedtime stories. Apparently its song does things. Which things sorta depends on who’s telling it. Anyway, look at her now. White marble, about two feet of it. Chest puffed out, neck stretched up, beak open. She’s about to let the whole room have it. Bird number one. He’ll keep making birds. About thirty of ’em. One ends up in federal court. That’s a whole different story. Anyway, now look under her. Not the block. Under the block. Two little stone people. Rough, barely carved, holding a rock on their heads. That was its own sculpture. He showed it in 1908. A couple years later, it’s holding up the bird. A sculpture holding up a sculpture. It starts here, and he does it the rest of his life.

title: THE RED STUDIO
transcript: Imagine Matisse in his studio. Before the red. He's already painted the room once. Blue walls. Pink floor. Yellow furniture. The real walls were white, by the way. He lives with the painting for a while. Then he goes back and does the thing that should wreck it. He covers almost the whole room in red. Not red in the room. Red as the room. Look what he doesn't paint over. His own art. The paintings and sculptures keep their colors while the room around them goes red. But why red? Right after he finished it, a visitor came by and went looking for the red wall. Matisse told him, "This wall does not exist at all!" Where the red came from, he said he didn't know. But he said everything in there only became what it was together with the red. So, let the red hit you first. Then you start finding things. The table. A green plant in a bottle. The chair, barely more than a line. The clock with no hands. And all these paintings inside the painting, still in color. Now, the man in Moscow who'd ordered it never saw the canvas. He asked for a little watercolor of it instead. Matisse sent one, with a letter. The red, he wrote, was a "harmonic link." The man wrote back: "It must be very interesting, but I now prefer your paintings with figures." Matisse kept it for about fifteen years. Then it drifted. Ended up on the wall of a London nightclub, the Gargoyle. Eventually it came to this museum. And when it did, a painter named Mark Rothko started coming here. Just to stand in front of it. For hours. He said when you looked at it, you became the color. You became totally saturated with it.

title: I AND THE VILLAGE
transcript: Alright, here we go. A guy with a bright green face, nose to nose with a cow. And they're dead serious about it. Locked eyes, a thin line drawn right between them like they're hashing something out. Then, for no reason, there's a tiny woman milking a cow, tucked into its cheek. Inside its face. Sure. Up in the corner, some lady floats by upside down, sawing at a violin. A house sits on its roof. Nobody in here finds any of this the least bit strange. So. Chagall grew up dirt poor in a tiny Jewish village called Vitebsk. The kind of place where you basically lived on top of your animals. A cow wasn't dinner, it was a guy you knew. You fed it, milked it, grew up next to it. So him, going eye to eye with this animal like equals? That's not a gag. That's how close it was. Now, everybody wants to call this a dream. He hated that. Not a dream, he said. Memory. And memory's a mess. It doesn't line up like a photo. It's everything at once, all the wrong sizes, the important stuff glowing, things floating loose because in your head there's no up, no down, no clock. He's not painting the village. He's painting what it feels like to remember it. By now he's in Paris, surrounded by Cubists chopping the world into tidy gray cubes. And instead of joining them, he paints this. Green and red and completely impossible. Home, the way it lived inside him. And here's what the painting couldn't know yet. Within Chagall's lifetime, the Holocaust would all but erase this whole world. The crooked little houses. The fiddler. The cow that was a guy you knew. The people. Gone. He painted it before any of it happened. Which makes this one of the last places it's still alive. A green man, a cow, and everything he couldn't stand to lose.

title: STILL LIFE WITH AUBERGINES
transcript: The eggplants have got a lot of competition. Look at that blue and green behind them. Huge curls, leaves, flowers. Taking up most of the painting. Then over on the right, a strip of yellow with little bunches of flowers running down it. Apparently, one floral pattern wasn't enough. Down below, an orange table tips up toward us. Two green pears on a white plate. A big pink vase with handles curling out at the sides. And tucked beside it, that little pale plaster figure. An anatomy model, with the muscles showing. You almost lose him in the upholstery. Then right at the front, three dark purple eggplants. Stretched out on the orange. There they are. Now look at how loosely he's painted all this. The blue skips. The orange has gaps. Pale canvas shows through everywhere. Nothing's polished up for company. And the pattern gets as much attention as the things we're supposed to be looking at. Your eye goes off following a curl, and suddenly you've forgotten the vegetables. Even front and back start to go. The whole thing turns into one big patchwork. It ought to be a headache. Flowers, scrolls. Pattern on top of pattern. But Matisse grew up around textiles, in the weaving towns of northern France. This stuff was familiar. So stand here a second. There's a lot to look at. But somehow, no hurry. This is the guy who said he wanted his art to be like a good armchair. Something a tired person could sink into. And apparently, you can get there by putting a pattern on practically everything that'll hold still. Pleasure for the eyes. That sounds harmless enough. But "decorative" was a put-down. A way of saying a painting wasn't serious. Just wallpaper. Beautiful wallpaper. Wrapped around three eggplants. A few months later, he shows paintings like this in Paris. And what does he call them? In his words: "Decorative sketches."

title: JEANNETTE (III)
transcript: Check these out. Start at the end with the one that still looks like a person. Then work your way down. That's Jeanne. In the first one, a face you could imagine meeting. Soft cheeks. Everything more or less where you'd expect it. The second one's still her. A little firmer. Things are getting pushed around, but you'd know her on the street. Then the third. Now something's happening. By the fourth, the features are turning into lumps. Heavy ones. And the fifth. One eye's practically a glob. The nose is a blade. And what is going on at the top of her head? From the right angle, the whole thing's basically a bronze maraca. But look back down the row. He keeps changing what gets to be big. What gets to stick out. What he can get rid of. A cheek becomes a lump. A nose becomes an edge. He's treating a face like something he can rearrange. Which, in clay, it is. Matisse said sculpture helped him sort out his ideas for painting. Apparently, sometimes you have to work on somebody's head to get your own straight. Five versions over six years. Like he's trying to figure out which wrong one's the right one. You keep looking for Jeanne. Even in that last one. A bit of a face here, something almost familiar there. How far can he push it before you stop seeing somebody? He stopped at five. But she only sat for the first two. After that, he worked from the heads he'd already made. So we're watching him change a sculpture of a woman. Then change the sculpture again. By the fifth, he's taken off a clump of hair, built up the brow, stretched the neck. And he built it on a plaster cast of the third. Apparently, you're allowed to skip one.

title: HOMAGE TO JS BACH
transcript:
There's a name printed on this one.

BACH.

Block capitals, a J and an S underneath. Not painted freehand. Stenciled, the way you'd letter a shipping crate.

The least readable style of painting anybody ever invented, and the one thing you can read is the part he didn't draw. You can see it from across the room.

And the whole painting is smaller than a card table.

Watch what the letters do. Everything around them splinters. Violin scrolls, strings, shards. The letters just sit there. Flat on the surface, refusing to play along.

The cheapest trick here is the one telling the truth.

This whole thing is a flat piece of canvas.

Now look at the left edge. See those ochre stripes, combed like oak?

Braque knew how to do that because Braque painted houses.

His father painted houses. His grandfather painted houses. Georges did the real apprenticeship, ladders and all. Decorator work. Fake wood grain, fake marble. Making cheap walls look expensive.

No brush did that. That's a decorator's graining comb dragged through wet paint. The grooves are still in there.

Far as anyone can tell, this is where fake wood grain enters Cubism.

It got in because Braque owned the comb.

Of course he did. He painted houses.

Why Bach? Braque actually played. Flute, piano. His dealer swore he claimed he could get through Beethoven symphonies on an accordion.

And Bach was his favorite. Past that, he never said.

Then look at the other name. Bottom left, in cursive: G Braque. Something he hardly ever did in these years.

Bach. Braque.

Pretty good. For a house painter.

title: MAN WITH A GUITAR
transcript: Alright, so. Try to find the guitar. Take your time. It's in there. The man too, somewhere in that pile of gray-brown planes. Now look at the top left corner. There's a nail. Little coil of rope hanging off it, painted so sharp you could reach up and unhook it. A whole man, broken into a hundred shards, and the realest thing in here is the nail. Not the guy. Braque loved this move. One perfect little real-world thing, almost hiding in there. Pretty great, right? Now think about what a guitar even is. It's a music thing. And music, you never get all at once. You hear one note, then the next, then the next, and somewhere in there your brain glues it into a song. You never hold the whole thing. It's always in pieces, always moving. So Braque looks at that and goes, fine. That's how I'll paint it. In pieces. Over time. He's making your eyes do what your ears already do. And maybe that's why the nail's there. The one thing that won't move, while everything else is basically sound. It's like something to grab onto. And look at that rope again. The real one, on the nail. Because by now Braque and Picasso are so deep into this together you can't tell whose hand did what. Studios down the street. Every day. Same problem, two guys coming at it from opposite sides. He called it being "two mountaineers, roped together." Then 1914. The war calls him up. A year later he gets shrapnel to the head. Somehow he survives, but he's gone from painting for months, and by the time he's back, Picasso's moved on without him. But that rope, it's still there hanging on the nail.

title: THE ARCHITECT'S TABLE
transcript: This is called The Architect's Table. Except, there's no architect. Honestly, there's barely a table. There's an oval. And inside it, there's a pipe. A bottle. A wine glass. Some sheet music. And a set square. Or, you know, pieces of all those things. Picasso's Cubism has gotten to the point where everything is disappearing into this brown fog of edges and angles. You grab for an object and it kind of slips away. Except, there are two women hiding in here. You don't get their faces. You get their names. The first one, you can't miss. MA JOLIE. Big block letters right across the sheet music. Means "my pretty one." It's from a popular song at the time. But it's also Picasso's nickname for his lover, Eva Gouel. So Eva gets the billboard. And Gertrude? Gertrude gets a calling card. Look down in the lower right. Tiny little painted card. Miss Gertrude Stein. So, one winter day, she stops by Picasso's studio. He's not there. She leaves her card. And Picasso just... paints the thing straight into the picture. Which is such a strange little detail. One woman gets giant letters. The other barely gets a signature. The lover, he shouts. The visitor, he whispers. And then, okay, here's the ending. A couple years later, Gertrude buys the painting. First Picasso she ever bought completely on her own. Her name was already in it.

title: DYNAMISM OF A SOCCER PLAYER
transcript: Okay. Somewhere in here there's a soccer player. Good luck with that one! Six and a half feet of orange and blue going off like a grenade, and a guy who's been more or less deleted by his own speed. These are the Futurists. Italy, around 1913, completely high on the future. Engines, speed, machines, anything loud and new and fast. And they hated the past so much they wanted the museums burned down. Called them cemeteries. Boccioni was their big painter, and the whole point was to kill the one thing painting always did. Hold a body still so you can look at it. He wanted the opposite. Make it move. Make it come apart. They had other plans too. Figured a good war would scrub the world clean and start it fresh. So when the real one showed up, they signed up thrilled. Here's how that goes for the painter of pure speed. He's thirty-three, in training, and he falls off a horse. Not the war. A horse. The fastest mind in Italy, taken out by the slowest thing in the army. And yeah, some of this future-worship runs straight into Fascism later. So no, you don't get to call it innocent. But the painting still works. That's the uncomfortable part. The player's still in there. Still moving. The one thing in the whole building that won't hold still. Which is exactly what they wanted. They just didn't picture the wall. White paint, a guard a few feet off, a little label with his name. One of the cemeteries they swore they'd burn. Permanent collection now.

title: THE BLUE WINDOW
transcript: This whole thing is blue. The walls, the table, the trees, the sky. That deep, dreamy blue, right across the picture. Now, a window is supposed to give you a view. You're in here. The garden's out there. Fairly basic arrangement. So watch what he does with it. Try to find where the bedroom stops and the garden begins. There are clues. But that blue keeps getting in the way. The dressing table up front and the trees out back just melt into each other. The tabletop and the sky, made of the same stuff. Once, on the radio, somebody asked Matisse why he kept painting windows. His answer was basically, what inside? What outside? From the horizon right into his studio, he saw it as one space. This is the Matisses' bedroom. That's his wife Amélie's dressing table. Her flowers, her green lamp, her little brooch in a dish down in the corner. All her things, just sitting there. And he's soaked it all in blue. Funnily enough, the Nazis couldn't stand it. They pulled it off a museum wall in Germany and branded it degenerate. Some flowers. A lamp. A little brooch. Apparently, a menace. Anyway. Back in the blue. See that pale building out the window? The one with the dab of yellow? That's his studio. This is the only painting where he showed that studio from the outside. And when this picture appeared in a Paris magazine in 1914, it had a different name. La Glace sans tain. A mirror without the silver backing. Take that away, and you can see straight through it. A window.

title: AGAPANTHUS
transcript: Look at those stems lean. Long arcs, little purple flowers at the ends. Green everywhere. They're Agapanthus. Monet planted them along his pond at Giverny. He starts the big pond paintings in his seventies. This is one of them. Oh, and he's doing very well at this point. Six full-time gardeners. He's bought the house, expanded the grounds, made a water garden. A Japanese bridge, the whole thing. So, he's got the garden. He's got the money. But his eyes are giving him trouble. Cataracts. He says he's choosing paints by the labels on the tubes. Think about that. Monet. Checking which one's blue. Meanwhile, one of his closest friends is Georges Clemenceau. France's prime minister during the last year of the First World War. Also the minister of war. And he gardens. As if he doesn't have enough going on. He's the one who talks Monet into giving the big pond paintings to France. As a kind of victory present. Twenty-two of them end up in oval rooms in Paris. And for years, Clemenceau's on him about the eyes. Get them operated on. He'd trained as a doctor, too. Anyway, look back at those purple flowers. All that green. Clemenceau writes him: "You taught me to understand light." In that same letter he says: "My eyes need your color."

title: WATER LILIES
transcript: See that pale bit in the middle? Those are clouds. Now look at the lily pads next to them. The leaves are sitting on the water. The clouds are reflected in it. You know that. But try looking at both. Follow the cloud for a second and the water gets deep. Then you catch a leaf, and there's the surface again. Same bit of painting. So the term "Impressionism" is named after one of Monet's paintings. Basically, the light changes, the colors change. He made a whole career out of paying attention. And here he's given you nearly forty-two feet to get lost in. Three big panels. Pale blue and lavender opening up in the middle, darker greens and purples gathering at the ends. No horizon. No strip of bank. He's left out the things that would tell you where you are. So you're looking down at a pond, looking up at the sky, without moving your head. Pretty good from a bench, right? Go closer and something else happens. The water disappears into paint. Thick bits. Scrubby bits. One color dragged over another. He built a huge studio to make these. Worked on them in there for years, moving between them, painting things over. Looks like a passing cloud. But, you know, took him a while. Then you sit back down, and there's the pond again. Oh, so the actual pond wasn't quite this peaceful. There were trains going past the garden. You don't get those in here. And the road by the pond left dust all over the lilies. So Monet had a gardener go out in a boat and clean them. Somebody had to literally dust the pond. After he died, these stayed in his studio for decades. Then in the fifties, painters like Pollock are working huge. Paint everywhere. Your eye moving across the whole canvas. And so this museum takes another look at the old man's pond.

title: GARE MONTPARNASSE (THE MELANCHOLY OF DEPARTURE)
transcript: Okay. We got a train station. A clock up on a brick tower. Stuck at twenty-seven past one. An empty square. A little train on the horizon, puffing smoke. Two tiny figures way off, just standing there. And down in the corner, a pile of bananas. Green ones. Not even ripe. Just sitting there like they know something. For about one second, it all looks normal. Then it tips. Look at the ground on the right, ramping up too steep, too fast. The arcade on the left pulls one way, the building behind it pulls another. The wind's whipping the flags on that tower. But the train's smoke goes straight up. Nothing lines up. That's the trick. The bananas are a decoy. The thing crawling up your back is the geometry. He built a place that can't exist, and painted it like it's the most normal thing in the world. And he called it The Melancholy of Departure. Like, you can't even tell if that train's coming or going, but you already miss it. He painted it in early 1914. Here's the kicker. De Chirico is twenty-five. Twenty-five, and he's already found a frequency nobody else can hear yet. Empty plazas. Long shadows. Ya know that feeling when nobody's following you, but you pick up the pace anyway. A few years later, the Surrealists find this. Dalí, Magritte, Ernst, all of them walk through this exact door. And by the time they move in, he's gone. He drops the whole thing, goes classical, starts painting like it's three hundred years ago. They turn on him. But, the painting already did its job. It built the room. They moved in later. He'd already moved out. A few years later, he finds out these early paintings are still the ones people want. So he makes more. Sometimes he gives the new ones old dates. This one really is from 1914. Some of the later ones? Same artist. But wrong year. There's an Italian word for them. Verifalsi. True fakes.

title: TABLEAU NO. 2 / COMPOSITION NO. V
transcript: Mondrian is thirty-nine when he moves to Paris. And almost immediately, he drops a letter from his name. Mondriaan used to have two a's. Paris gets one. Small change. But that's the idea. Ya know, New city. New painter. Sure. He gets deep into what Picasso and Braque are doing. Take a face or a guitar apart and spread it across a canvas. But, Mondrian wants to see what happens if you keep going. This painting probably started as a church. Notre-Dame-des-Champs, near Montparnasse. Not the famous Notre Dame. A neighborhood church. But by the time Mondrian is finished, the subject is barely hanging on. Black lines run into each other, stop, and start again. Pink. Dusty yellow. Gray. It's called Tableau no. 2 / Composition no. V. Two titles. Neither one admits it's a church. A critic saw it in March 1914 and called it a map. Or a labyrinth. Fair. Try following a black line from one side to the other. Nobody said church. Then Mondrian picks a terrible summer to go home. His father is sick, so he heads back to Holland for a visit. That same summer, over in The Hague, he gets the first show of his own he's ever had. Sixteen paintings. Somebody buys this one. It closes July thirty-first. Four days later, the war starts. And now he can't get back to Paris. He has no studio. No painting materials. No income. For more than a year, he mostly draws. Down on the Dutch coast, he starts working on the North Sea. Except those seascapes get stripped down too. The water becomes horizontal strokes. The pier gives him vertical ones. He's doing to the sea what he'd been doing to the church. Working out how much of the actual thing he can lose. Check the corners on this one. The middle is packed. Out there it thins down to almost nothing. Just gray canvas. It never makes it to the edge. The visit lasts five years.

title: GUITAR
transcript: For as long as there's been sculpture, there were basically two ways to make one. You carve it out of stone, or you model it in clay and cast it. Either way you start with a solid lump and find the thing inside. Picasso looks at all that and goes, nah. He grabs flat scraps. Cardboard, paper, string. Later, cut sheet metal. And he builds a guitar. Doesn't carve it, doesn't mold it. He assembles it, like a kid with a cereal box, out of bent flat pieces and empty air. Nobody had really made a sculpture this way before. He basically invents building one instead of carving one. And a hundred years of modern sculpture walks through the door he just opened. Now look at the sound hole. On a real guitar that's a hole. A dark round nothing in the middle. Picasso makes it a little tube that sticks straight out at you. He took the empty part and turned it into the solid part. The hole pokes out like a nose. Sounds like a gag. It's not. He'd been looking at an African mask where the eyes poke out at you instead of sinking in, and he stole the logic. Flip it inside out. The nothing becomes the thing. It's cardboard and tin and string. Looks like it took an afternoon. And it quietly rewired what sculpture was allowed to be. Years from now, an old man builds a whole goat out of garbage. Starts right here. A flat tin guitar with a hole that sticks out.

title: PAINTERLY REALISM OF A BOY WITH A KNAPSACK
transcript: Okay so. The title of this thing is longer than the actual painting. You ready? "Painterly Realism of a Boy with a Knapsack. Color Masses in the Fourth Dimension." And the painting? A black square. And a little red one. That's it. That's the whole thing. So, uh, where's the boy. Where's the knapsack. Yeah, there's no boy. Never was gonna be one. He sticks this giant cosmic name on two little squares on purpose, and that gap, between the huge title and the two shapes, that's the bit. Except he's not kidding. He means every word. This is 1915. He's just cooked up a thing he calls Suprematism. His own description: he'd boiled himself down to "the zero of form" and "escaped from the circle of things." Which, translated out of guru, means a painting doesn't have to be a picture of anything anymore. No boy, no apple, no saint. Just shapes. Just color. Hanging there. And get this. He called it realism. Straight up. "New painterly realism," his phrase. Like, two squares are more real than a painting of a boy, not less. And, honestly? Kind of has a point. The squares aren't faking anything. They're not pretending to be a guy, or a window, or a nice day in the country. A square's just a square. Can't lie to you. So look at 'em. Big black square. Little red one. Tipped a bit, floating on all that white. He's not painting a thing. He's painting a thing with nothing in it. And here's the real move. The show where these first go up, 1915, he sticks a plain black square way up high in the corner of the room. Now, in a Russian house, that corner's got exactly one job. It's where the religious icon goes. The holy picture. So everybody who walks in just gets it. He's not hanging a painting. He's hanging a religion. A black square, right where God used to be. So, yeah. Either it's the most pretentious thing a person's ever done with a ruler and two colors. Or it's one of the gutsiest. With this guy, it's both. He looked at everything painting had ever done, all the kings and saints and bowls of fruit, and just went, nah. Start over. From a black square. And a name three sizes too big.

title: THE PIANO LESSON
transcript: This one, you need the year. It's 1916. France is deep in the war. Matisse tried to enlist when it started. Even bought the boots. They turned him down. Twice. Too old, they said. Forty-four. And a weak heart. His mother's alone in the occupied north. His brother's in a prison camp in Germany. His two boys are getting close to military age. And he's at home. Painting his sixteen-year-old son, Pierre, at the piano. It's eight feet tall. That's a lot of canvas for piano practice. Now look at how much room there is around him. All that grey. And Pierre's little head down on the right, just clearing the music. One eye looking out. The other disappears into that dark triangle cutting across his face. Up above him, another figure sits bolt upright. Hands in her lap. No face at all. She looks like she's making sure he practices. And down in the opposite corner, a little bronze-colored sculpture. Another seated woman, all curves and elbows. So he's got company. Nobody's saying much. On the left, a long wedge of green. The garden, squeezed into a triangle. Below it, the iron railing curls around. Those curves turn up again on the music stand. Little bits of decoration in this very severe room. Then that great pink piano cuts across the bottom. And behind it, the boy. We're getting into Picasso territory here. Flat planes, hard edges. Matisse took what he wanted from Cubism and never really joined the club. And here he is, using it on his own kid. A kid practicing piano. An ordinary afternoon. So why does it feel like this? You can't know how much of the war got into the picture. But once you know what's happening to his family, that grey starts to feel different. Look at the metronome on the piano. The little thing that ticks to keep you in time. Another triangle. Like the wedge over his eye. The boy has to keep up with it. And you can almost hear it, in all that grey. Tick. Tick. Tick. The next summer, Matisse writes to his painter friend Camoin. "Something important has happened in my house." "Jean, my eldest, has left to join the regiment at Dijon."

title: FROM THE VIADUCT, 125TH STREET, NEW YORK
transcript: Okay. 1916. A twenty-five-year-old kid hauls a camera the size of a suitcase up onto a viaduct over 125th Street. And instead of pointing it out at the city, like a normal person, he aims it straight down. At the sidewalk. He didn't make any of this. He found it. The shadow was really there. The light actually did that. Two men really were standing on that corner, mid-conversation. A painter could invent a scene like this. Strand had to catch one. And he's got maybe a couple minutes before the sun moves and it's gone. Look what he goes for. Not the street. Not the two guys. The shadow. That big dark web of girders crossing the pavement. He aimed a machine built to record the truth at a sidewalk, and came back with pure geometry. He didn't photograph a place. He photographed a shape. And in 1916, that's not what photographs do. A photo's supposed to be a picture of something. A person, a view, a moment you keep. Strand hands you an abstraction. Stieglitz, the most powerful man in American photography, takes one look and gives this kid the entire last issue of his magazine, Camera Work. Like: everybody, look. This is where it's going. And here's the wild part. It's all real. Soft and hazy as it is, every line in it actually happened. For a few minutes, on a corner nobody'd look at twice, the city folded into a diagram. And this kid was up there, looking down, ready. Click. Gone. Except he kept it.

title: THE MOROCCANS
transcript: Kind of a strange one... coming from the color guy. Look at all that black. A big empty field of it, right through the middle. Matisse spent two winters in Tangier, in Morocco. And then back in France, he painted what he remembered. He was always going south for the light. And down there, it's brutal. So... we've got three big sections, all sort of elbowing into the black. Up on the left, a white dome behind a balcony. A kind of flowerpot on the rail. Below that, a whole pile of green shapes. Round peachy things tucked in among them. Underneath, a crooked white grid, almost like a tiled floor. And over on the right, all that dusty pink, almost kind of mauve. Inside of that, a man in a white turban and a blue robe, with his back to us. The colors are quieter than you'd expect. Chalky whites, dull greens, that worn-looking blue. Now, those green lumps. Melons on the vine? Or the bowed backs and heads of men kneeling in prayer? Matisse said melons. Watermelons and gourds, he called them. Other people see men praying. You can flip between them all day. He'd been carrying the idea around for four years. He sketched it in a letter home to his wife, from Tangier, in 1912. By the time he finished the painting, it was 1916. He was in a studio outside Paris. And at Verdun, French and German soldiers were dying by the thousands. And there's all that black. Easy to read it as gloom. But that's not how Matisse explained it. Thirty-odd years later, he said this was where his blacks began. Black didn't have to mean shadow. Or night. It depended on the colors around it. Get those relationships right, and black could be part of the light, same as white. He wrote that the big black in his Moroccans glowed as brightly as any color in it. He'd painted light with it. Even the light of Tangier.

title: FOUNTAIN
transcript: Okay, so this is the urinal they wouldn't let into a show that was supposed to let everybody in. Grand Central Palace, New York. 1917. They're putting up more than two thousand artworks, all in alphabetical order. And the directors are sitting in a meeting, arguing about a urinal. It's on a pedestal. The fee's been paid. It's signed R. Mutt. Some of them say it's indecent. The others say, hold on. We promised no jury, no prizes. You pay the fee, you're in. So they vote. Now, officially, they never reject it. They just put it behind a partition. One of the directors quits over this. His name is... Marcel Duchamp. So you're probably thinking... who sent it in? We'll get to that. First, look at the thing. It's a men's room urinal, lying on its back. And there on the rim, in black paint: "R. Mutt, 1917." Duchamp said later that he wanted the object with "the least chance of being liked." Then he and some friends put out this little magazine. They print Alfred Stieglitz's photograph of the thing. The only picture of the original, and next to it, an unsigned editorial. Whether Mr. Mutt made it with his own hands, it says, "has no importance. He chose it." And then, in the same editorial: "The only works of art America has given are her plumbing and her bridges." In 2004, a poll asks five hundred art experts to name the most influential modern artwork. Guess what wins? Picasso comes in second. But go back to that name on the rim. The day after the show opens, Duchamp writes to his sister. He says "one of my female friends" sent in a urinal under a man's name. He never says who. The papers had Mr. Mutt down as some guy in Philadelphia. Some say it was the Baroness Elsa, a Dada artist who was living in Philly that year. Nobody's settled it. So that name, the one thing painted on the thing, might not even be his. And the original? Gone... To be honest, it's kind of crazy how many of this guy's things get lost. Anyways, in 1950, a gallery wants to show it. So Duchamp has the dealer buy a used one in Paris, and he paints the R. Mutt on it himself. By 1964, there's an edition of eight. That's what the museums have. But back in 1917, just a couple of weeks after the show opens, Stieglitz writes to a friend about his photograph. Everyone who's seen it, he says, thinks it's beautiful. "A cross between a Buddha and a veiled woman."

title: COMPOSITION WITH COLOR PLANES 5
transcript: Pink. That's the first problem. You think you know Mondrian. Red. Yellow. Blue. Thick black lines. This one has pink. No black. Not even a proper grid. It's 1917. The Mondrian in your head hasn't been invented yet. He's living in Laren, a village in Holland. Nearby is another painter named Bart van der Leck. Van der Leck had worked in stained glass. So he already knew what color looked like when it didn't have to pretend to be skin or sky or a vase. Red could just be red. Yellow could just be yellow. Mondrian's own paintings were doing something else. The trees and oceans were disappearing. You had to work harder and harder to find what the painting had started as. Each man sees the part he doesn't have. So they start stealing from each other. Mondrian takes the color. Van der Leck takes the nerve to let the subject disappear. Fair trade. And for a minute, they meet right here. Composition with Color Planes 5. One big mustard-yellow block in the middle. Pink and gray around it. The white isn't background. It cuts in between the colors. And nobody has built the black fence yet. That same year, they help start a magazine. De Stijl. "The Style." Not "A Style." "The." That is a lot of confidence for a group still deciding whether pink stays. The next year, there's a manifesto to sign. Mondrian signs it. Van der Leck doesn't. He helped invent "The Style." He just didn't agree with the rules. Van der Leck eventually lets recognizable things back in. Trees. Flowers. A man on a horse. Mondrian goes the other way. He keeps getting stricter. The black grid arrives. The pink goes.

title: WHITE ON WHITE
transcript: “Swim in the white free abyss, infinity is before you.” That’s Kazimir Malevich. This is one of his white paintings. A white square on a white square. Which sounds like nothing. So, look closer. The background’s warm, almost cream. The square’s cool, almost gray. Tipped a little. A few years before, he paints a black square on white. He calls it Suprematism. Basically, a painting doesn’t have to show anything anymore. Shapes and colors alone can make you feel something. Then he goes further. Even the black goes. Okay, so, quick history lesson. After the Russian Revolution, the new government hands guys like Malevich their own art schools. Ten years later, Stalin’s taking over. And they want paintings everybody can, ya know… understand. So… Malevich takes about seventy works to a show in Berlin. A month in, he gets called back home. And he figures he’s in trouble. He even writes a will, in case he ends up dead, or in prison. And he leaves the paintings with an architect friend. He never sees them again. Three years later, the man who painted nothing gets arrested. Questioned about that trip. Let go. And this one? The architect passes them to a museum man. When the Nazis come in, he puts them in storage. So this “free abyss” is now sitting in the dark. Then this guy Alfred Barr, from the brand-new Museum of Modern Art, comes through and buys two. This one included. He sneaks them over the border. In a suitcase, and a couple of canvases rolled up inside his umbrella. Was this one in the umbrella? Nobody knows. But the painting gets out. That same year, Malevich dies. His friends drive his coffin down the main street on an open truck. And on the front of the truck… a black square.

title: ENDLESS COLUMN, VERSION I
transcript: One shape. A wooden bead, fat in the middle, pinched at both ends. Stack it. Then stack it again. That's the whole sculpture. Oak, carved in 1918, with the chisel marks still in it. Half totem pole, half stack of diamonds. Now look at the top. The last shape gets cut off halfway through. Same at the bottom. That's not damage. That's the whole idea. It doesn't end. It just stops. And your eye keeps stacking the pieces right past the ceiling. Try not to do it. You can't. He figured out how to make you build the rest. And there's no pedestal. Sculptures usually stand on something. This one just stands. Or maybe it is the pedestal. Just with nothing on top. Brancusi had used this shape underneath other sculptures. Then, at some point, he realized he didn't need the sculpture anymore. The repeating could be the whole thing. Then the shape waits twenty years. In 1935, the Women's League of Gorj asks Brancusi to make a war memorial. Gorj is his county. He was born there. In 1916, German forces had come for the bridge at Targu Jiu. The town held it. Not just the garrison. Old men, boys and women picked up whatever they had and kept them off the crossing until the army arrived. Most war memorials give you a general on a horse. Brancusi gives them this. The same shape, now cast in iron, almost a hundred feet tall. The pieces climb until the iron runs out, and then your eye takes over. A column with no end, for people who ended. Before it became that, it was this. Six feet eight inches of carved oak. The moment Brancusi realized a pedestal could keep going forever.

title: THE CITY
transcript: Okay. Quick Léger fact. He spent three years of the war digging trenches in the Argonne. Shells going over his head the whole time. And the thing he wrote about wasn't the fear. It was the breech of a 75 millimeter cannon with the sun on it. "The magic of light on the white metal." His words. The deadliest object in France, and he's standing there thinking, that is gorgeous. Then he gets gassed, spends a year in a hospital, and comes home. And this is what he paints about it. The City. 1919. No trenches anywhere. Billboards. Scaffolding. A staircase. A giant letter B with no word attached. Full volume. Now find the people. Two of them, down by the stairs, dead center. Flat. Dark. No faces. Then look at the posters. The blue guy in the billboard on the right has more color than the actual humans. Maybe that's a complaint. Doesn't feel like one. Feels like a man who walked out of the war still in love with the machine that almost killed him. He just stopped pretending people stood outside it. There's no horizon in here, by the way. No place to stand, no view. There's even a big purple pole planted right in the middle, blocking the best part. Cities do that. You don't look at this city. It hits you. Which is the honest version. Nobody sees a city. You're just in one, and it's loud, and somewhere a sign is shouting half a word at you. He thought all that was worth loving. Stand here a minute. Hard not to.

title: SPATIAL CONSTRUCTION NO. 12
transcript: Alright, Rodchenko. The great quitter of modern art. The guy doesn't drift away from stuff, he just ends it. A year or so after this, he puts up three canvases in Moscow. One's just red. One's just yellow. One's just blue. And he announces, that's it, it's all over. Painting, taken to its logical conclusion. His words. Then he actually quits. Walks off, makes ads, takes pictures. This is also a man who designed his own work jumpsuit, pockets everywhere for the tools, had his wife sew it, and wore it to teach his classes. Because that was the whole idea after the Revolution. No more genius in a smock. An artist is an engineer now. They even called themselves Constructivists. Builders. So look what the engineer built. One flat sheet of plywood. That's it, that's the material. Ovals drawn inside ovals, cut out, fanned into space, tied with wire. The whole recipe fits on an index card. Which was the point. He doesn't even give it a title, he gives it a number. Spatial Construction number 12. Like a part in a catalog. And it hangs from the ceiling, because pedestals were for the old guys. Get up close, look at the inner rings. Still kind of silver, right? Aluminum paint. It was supposed to catch the light while it turned, he called the series Light-Reflecting Surfaces. The outer rings are back to plain wood. That part's just time. Now, 1921. A room in Moscow, hung full of these things. The big show, the one that launched them. Everything we know about that room comes from two photographs. Two. Almost nothing in those pictures still exists. One little piece by another guy. And this. Funny thing, though. You could build one of these tonight. Same sheet, same cuts, same wire. And it wouldn't count. Everyone knows it wouldn't. Only the original counts. Which is the exact feeling Rodchenko spent his life trying to kill. It grew back anyway. On this one. Not bad for an index card.

title: THE NEWBORN, VERSION I
transcript: Alright, so this one’s small. About eight inches long. Get your face down to its level. First thing you’ll think is probably… spaceship thing. Or… some kinda droid egg. It’s from 1920 and it looks like it hasn’t even been invented yet. And be honest. If nobody was watching, you’d probably pocket it. Anyway, look at the front. It’s got one slice taken off. A flat plane tilted up. And a little curl left over at the bottom. That curl is a chin. The slice is a mouth, wide open. It’s a baby! Well… sort of. If you’ve ever held one, you know this shape. The whole head goes mouth. The guy is Constantin Brancusi. Romanian, living in Paris. One of the guys who basically invented modern sculpture. And he’s been making children’s heads for years. Around 1906, a sleeping kid. Realistic. You’d know what you were looking at from across the room. Then he just keeps going with it. Head after head, and every time, something’s gone. Neck, gone. Hair, gone. The ears. The nose. By 1915, he’s down to this. An egg with a cry coming out of it. That one he cut out of marble. This is the bronze. Five years later. Same shape. Polished like a mirror. He gives this one away, by the way. In the summer of ’27. To a woman in New York. As a present. A screaming baby. MoMA bought it off her in ’43. It’s shiny. So… get close and your own face is in the scream.

title: THREE MUSICIANS
transcript: Look at these guys. Three of them, crammed together, mid-song. Big. Bright. Having a blast. And then you find out who they might be. And it stops being quite so fun. The harlequin in the middle, the one in the diamonds, that's Picasso. On the guitar. He painted himself as the harlequin over and over, so that one's pretty hard to miss. The other two, nobody can prove it, but they've usually been read as his two close friends. The poet Apollinaire, in the white Pierrot getup, on the clarinet. And the other poet, Max Jacob, dressed as a monk, with the sheet music. By the time Picasso paints this, Apollinaire's dead. Died young, two days before the war ended. Max Jacob's still around. But that same year, he'd left Paris and gone off to live near a monastery. Basically, like a monk. So Picasso's got one friend who's dead. One friend who's gone. And what does he do?
