So, the plan is to send her to another institution, in South Africa. But in Lisbon, she somehow gets away and reaches the Mexican embassy. A diplomat she knew, Renato Leduc, marries her so she can get out of Europe. She reaches New York. And in 1942, she paints this. So. Look at the woman. Wrapped from her neck to her ankles in something that looks like cowhide. Her arms pinned inside. Eyes closed. A crown of spikes. And she's standing inside a circle drawn on the grass. People often read her as Carrington herself. And beside her, that purple thing that looks a little like a heart. Some kind of pot, with two hairy legs and cloven hooves. Four little deer heads peeking out of the top. As if that's what's growing in it. Then look at the horse and the pregnant dog thing. Both have trees growing out of their tails. Follow the chains. Each is chained to the tree growing out of the other one. Neither's getting very far. And underneath this garden, right along the bottom, there's another whole world. Bats. Vultures. Things wrapped up like little bodies. All that beneath a beautifully kept lawn. She calls it Green Tea. Which clears up absolutely nothing. But look at the woman's wrapping again. It looks like a straitjacket. It also looks a little like a cocoon. Is she trapped in there, or is something changing?

title: BROADWAY BOOGIE WOOGIE
transcript: So, on his first night in New York, somebody puts on boogie-woogie for Mondrian. He's sixty-eight. The war has pushed him out of Paris, then London, and now he's starting over again. Boogie-woogie is Black American piano music. The left hand hammers out the same bass pattern. The right hand runs loose above it. One holds the floor under you. The other tries to get away. Mondrian had been working on that problem for years. Now it had a beat. A couple of years later, he makes this. A little over four feet square. White ground. Yellow lines, broken up by little blocks of red, blue, gray, and white. And no black. For years, thick black bars had kept Mondrian's colors apart. Here, color has to do the job itself. The grid is still there. It just won't sit still. He finishes it in 1943. He's seventy-one. It's the last painting he completes. But, there's one more going on the easel. He called it: Victory Boogie-Woogie. He keeps changing that one with little strips of colored tape. Move one. Peel another off. Try it somewhere else. When Mondrian dies, the tape is still attached. So, this is the last one he gets all the way into paint. And the same year he finishes it, Peggy Guggenheim puts him on a jury for a show of young American artists. The version that survives goes like this. Some unknown thirty-one-year-old submits a strange painting. Bright colors. A body lying down, maybe. Lines scratched across it like handwriting. Mondrian stands in front of it for a long time. Peggy comes over. "Pretty awful," she says. "That's not painting, is it?" Mondrian keeps looking. "I'm trying to understand what's happening here." Then he tells her: "I think this is the most interesting work I've seen so far in America." Peggy says, you can't compare this with the way you paint. Mondrian answers: "The way I paint and the way I think are two different things." The painting he was trying to understand was by Jackson Pollock.

title: CONSTELLATION WITH RED OBJECT
transcript: Nothing on this one moves. Which is a strange thing to say about a Calder. No motor. No balancing act. Just a handful of wooden shapes held out from the wall on stiff steel wire. A red almond. A black bowtie. A tall one like a chess piece somebody stretched. A little yellow bead way off on its own. This is Constellation with Red Object. Alright, it's 1943, Calder is in Connecticut. The war is on. Aluminum is going into airplanes and bombs. So he can't get much of it. A year earlier he had gone into his studio and pulled out an old sculpture called The Crowd. A group of people carved from ebony back in 1929. Then he destroyed it. Sawed it up. Carved the figures apart. Hung the pieces on wire and watched them turn. That's where this came from. Steel wire. Everything frozen in place, but spread out like it might keep going. The curator James Johnson Sweeney and a friend came up with a name for these things. Constellations. Calder offered half an explanation. Something about "cosmic nuclear gases." Then said he wasn't going to explain that either. This museum bought the piece the year he made it. There's another wooden Calder in this room. A rock, a couple of balls, and a crescent. Nothing on that one moves either. He carved it seven years before the war made metal scarce. They could ration his metal. They couldn't ration the stars.

title: THE SHE-WOLF
transcript: Alright... so, the year he painted this, Jackson Pollock had a day job. At a museum. It's 1943. He's thirty-one, doing maintenance and a little carpentry at what would become the Guggenheim. Back then, just a short walk from here. Never had a show of his own. And this is what he's painting. The She-Wolf. So, start at the left. Her nose nearly touches the edge. Head down, with that black line running along her back. Follow it across. Under the heavy belly, those little white hooks? Teats. Then a red line goes straight through her middle, like an arrow. Over on the right, patches of gray cover parts of her. There's a wolf to follow, but the paint keeps interrupting. Yellow, red, green. Lines crossing over her. And underneath the belly, some of that white has run straight down. The drip paintings he's known for are still a few years off. The drips aren't. That summer, another Guggenheim enters the story. Solomon's niece, Peggy. She has a gallery too. Offers him a contract: a hundred and fifty bucks a month. So now he can quit the day job. By November, she's given him his first solo show. The wolf's in it. The Times calls it obscurantism. Translation: he's being difficult on purpose. Then somebody putting a book together asks Pollock if he'd care to explain the wolf. His answer, more or less: he had to paint it. Trying to explain it would ruin it. So... that was the explanation. MoMA had its eye on her. According to Lee Krasner, who later married him, the museum puts a hold on the painting. Then decides the price is too high. Six hundred and fifty dollars. Then, needless to say... they somehow find the money. The first Pollock any museum ever buys. He's gone from doing maintenance in one museum to having a painting in another. In less than a year. And Peggy's gallery, the one that gave him that first show? It was called Art of This Century. Have a look at the name of this room.

title: TWO SISTERS
transcript: Alright, so John Graham said his father was Jupiter. Ya know. The god. Which makes the rest of his story sound fairly reasonable. So... he gets to New York in 1920. Back home, his name was Ivan Dombrowski. And the guy's got stories. An aristocratic family, a stint in the Tsar's cavalry. Then the revolution, prison, and an escape through Crimea. Some of that checks out. The bit about sharing a cell with the Tsar is... harder to follow. Even his birthplace is a problem. Usually it's Kyiv. But the baptism papers say Warsaw. Anyway. He learns to paint. He's already in his thirties. Then he writes a book about art. By 1942, a decorating firm asks him to put a show together. He hangs Picasso, Matisse and Braque alongside some local painters who haven't made much of a name for themselves. De Kooning. Lee Krasner. Jackson Pollock. Krasner hasn't even heard of Pollock. Goes over to his place to find out who this guy is. And two years later, Graham paints this. Two Sisters. Pearls. Jewels. Velvet. Like they've dressed for a Renaissance portrait, except nobody's quite got their top on. One's holding a pigeon. Look at that sleeve between them. Loose blue and yellow strokes, right next to all that flat pink skin. Then the hands. Parts are just pencil. Same with the belly and the ledge. Now the eyes. Both women. Cross-eyed. Graham said that helped hold the figures in place. Gave the painting more tension. More than Raphael's paintings, apparently. But then, he said, he lived in a more tense age. An acquaintance got a different explanation. That's what women's eyes did during an orgasm. According to Graham. Anyway, those younger painters start making their names. Graham goes the other way. Back to the old masters. Women like this. By 1946, he's writing The Case of Mr. Picasso. In his letters, he calls him a charlatan. Picasso. The guy he'd hung beside the Americans. Now he's a fraud. According to Graham. Some old friends are startled. They'd spent years listening to him. And Graham keeps going. Into alchemy. Astrology. Painting women with symbols drawn across their faces. Toward the end of his life, he says the paintings carry information. Occult knowledge. Things only a few people will know how to read.

title: SLOW SWIRL AT THE EDGE OF THE SEA
transcript: Look at this thing. Two strange little beings at the edge of the sea. All curls and stems, like they're doing some ceremony nobody remembers anymore. This is a Rothko. Yeah. That Rothko. Before the rectangles, this is what he was up to. Myths. Half-human things. Little creatures washed up from somewhere in his head. And there's a reason. Years later, Rothko said he couldn't use a normal human figure anymore without, his word, "mutilating" it. Which sounds like he wanted less human stuff in the paintings. He didn't. He wanted more. More feeling than some little painted person could carry. So for a while he tried creatures like these. Then even they weren't enough. That's the road to the rectangles. Not less human. Just no human standing there doing the acting for you. Now, 1944. Rothko is forty-one. Recently divorced. Barely known. And he meets Mary Alice Beistle. Mell. His son Christopher later said Rothko painted this for her, just after they met. Those two creatures? Christopher thought they were the two of them. Rothko and Mell, dancing around by the water. Not long after, they're married. And years later Christopher said this was the first painting he could remember. It hung over the couch in their family brownstone. Which is nice. Before all those floating rectangles... the family had floating creatures. Over the couch.

title: THE VERTIGO OF EROS
transcript: Alright, so look at the thin lines first. Kinda like perspective lines going nowhere. Somebody drew those with a ruler in his head. Chilean guy. Roberto Matta. Trained as an architect in Santiago. Goes to Paris. Draws for Le Corbusier. Ya know, one of the biggest names in modern architecture. Then the poet Lorca sends him to Dalí. Dalí sends him to André Breton. By ’37, he’s a Surrealist. One of the youngest in the group. Then the war. 1939, he gets to New York. He’s twenty-seven, about the same age as some of the young American painters. Motherwell. Pollock. By 1942, they’re meeting at his studio. He runs it like a class. Bring your drawings. Let the hand go. See what comes out. Motherwell said Matta wanted to show up the older Surrealists. The middle-aged, gray-haired guys, more or less. And the Americans take that let-the-hand-go part and run with it. Abstract Expressionism starts in rooms like that one. Anyway, back to the painting. He made it in 1944, and it’s big, right? Wider than a couch. Looks almost cosmic. Dark brown-black, with that yellow glow coming up from the bottom. It’s got these little white eggs floating through it. There’s that folded shape in the top left. Almost looks like pieces of a brain. Then there’s all this stuff scattered around them. Like a galaxy blew apart and the dust is still hanging there. Look at those thin lines again. White ones, yellow ones, traveling between all these things. Almost like somebody’s drawing the path of an orbit. Or trying to show you gravity. The invisible pull between things. You can see the architect’s trained hand is still in there. Drawing a space you can’t quite figure out. He called this kind of thing an inscape. A landscape inside his head. And somehow it feels miles deep. The title’s The Vertigo of Eros. Vertigo. Ya know, that feeling when you lose your balance. And Eros? That’s the Greek god of love and desire. OK, so there’s this guy Sigmund Freud. A doctor who thought a lot of what drives us is going on in our heads without us even knowing it. Freud borrows that name, Eros, to describe the pull toward life. Ya know, wanting to live. Love. Basically, just to keep going. And he thought there was an opposite pull, toward… death. So some people read this painting as those two forces pulling against each other. And you are somewhere in the middle, just trying to keep your balance. Now look for a floor in there. A horizon. Somewhere to put your feet. All those lines, but nowhere to stand.

title: DIARY OF A SEDUCER
transcript: First thing that hits you: it's gray. Not dead gray. Warm. Smoky. More like the color of being slightly outside yourself. There are bodies in here. Or pieces of them. Nothing quite finishes becoming a body. Then the yellow, buried in the gray like yolks. And then, just right of center, inside the black: It's looking at you. An eye, maybe. Could be an ear. White, almond-shaped, little lashes coming off it, with a red slit down the middle. Now look for red anywhere else. A smear at the bottom. Maybe another, if you hunt. But the hottest color in the painting is trapped inside that eye-ear thing. The last thing you notice is the wire. Thin, nervous lines floating over everything, tangled at the top like handwriting. Then you get the title. Diary of a Seducer. That's Kierkegaard. From a book called Either/Or. Basically the diary of a guy who turns desire into a full-time job. He studies it. Plans it. Watches himself feeling it. Not because he has to. Because that's the part he likes. Gorky painted this in 1945, during a year when his life finally seemed to be working. Married a few years. Two little daughters. After decades of nobody caring, the paintings were landing. His first major solo show. This is the part where you think: okay. He made it. And this is what he painted. Then everything goes bad, fast. A fire took a chunk of his work. Then cancer. A car crash broke his neck. Around the same time, his wife had an affair with Roberto Matta. There's a Matta hanging in this room, by the way. Three years after he painted this, Gorky took his own life in a shed in Connecticut. He was forty-four. So the gray isn't a warning. None of that had happened yet. Maybe this is just where he already stood. Slightly outside. Even in the good year. Even with everything working. Part of you is in it. Part of you is watching. Look where he put the red.

title: MILKY WAY
transcript: Brighton Beach, late 1930s. A grandmother in her forties picks up her son's paints. He's the one who wanted to be an artist. She'd raised five kids. Never took a class. Came over from Ukraine as a kid. A pogrom killed her father. Nothing in that resume says painter. Then she couldn't stop. Her name's Janet Sobel. She poured enamel. Tipped the canvas so it ran. Blew the wet stuff around through a tube. Look what that made. A pale web over the dark. Purple, blue, maroon under there. Big cream loops up top, like the rings a wet glass leaves on a bar. Yellow lace in the corners. Pink puddles down low. One black splat, off to the left, like a squashed bug. And thin white threads spraying off everything. That's probably where she blew on it. No center. No main event. Edge to edge. Milky Way, it's called. She signed it in cursive, lower left, like a check. Peggy Guggenheim hung her at Art of This Century, her gallery on Fifty-Seventh Street. Jackson Pollock saw her webs on the wall there. So did Clement Greenberg, the critic who championed Pollock. She got a solo show there in 1946. This one was in it. A reviewer said her pictures looked like marble, mother-of-pearl, spider webs and a spatter of milk. Then the story dropped her. Primitive, they said. A housewife. Turns out she was allergic to the paint. Tried to leave it alone. Couldn't, according to the Brooklyn Eagle. The family moves to Jersey. And by 1947, Pollock's making the drip paintings. The ones everybody knows. But years later, Greenberg lets something slip. He and Pollock had admired her paintings, he writes. "Rather furtively." Ya know, sneaking a peek at Grandma's stuff. He says hers were the first all-over paintings he'd ever seen. Paint carrying on right across the picture. Edge to edge. And Pollock? Admitted they'd made an impression on him. Then Greenberg gets to the next sentence. Pollock was already heading that way himself.

title: CHRISTINA'S WORLD
transcript: So... he saw her from inside that house. The one up the hill. It's 1948. Andrew Wyeth's upstairs in a farmhouse in Maine, using one of the rooms as a studio. He looks out the window. Down in the field, a woman's pulling herself through the grass. Using her arms. That's Christina Olson. She's fifty-five. The house belongs to her and her brother. She hasn't walked in years. Won't use a wheelchair. This is how she gets around the farm. And Wyeth knows her. He's been coming here for almost a decade. But when he paints this, he moves us. Down into the grass, behind her. Now we're looking up at the house he was looking out of. And he puts more field between her and home. And then there's Christina herself. The hands are hers. The thin arms. That pink dress. But his wife, Betsy, poses for the torso. She's twenty-six. Betsy gives it the name, too. Christina's World. He paints it in egg tempera. That's color mixed with egg yolk. All that grass, worked over in tiny strokes. Meanwhile, Pollock's got a canvas on the floor, pouring paint, and Wyeth's over here doing this. And when he finishes, he isn't sure it's any good. He later remembers thinking it was a flat tire. Then it goes to his dealer in New York. MoMA buys it. Eighteen hundred dollars. That flat tire becomes one of the best-known paintings in America. Wyeth becomes enormously popular. The critics aren't all buying it. One of them says, "He can't paint." Christina has a different complaint. Her face isn't in it. But according to Betsy, she also says, "Andy put me where I wanted to be." Christina dies in January 1968. Her brother had died the month before. Wyeth lives another forty-one years. When he dies in 2009, he's buried in the Olsons' little family cemetery. Down the hill from that house. With Christina.

title: NO. 1 (UNTITLED)
transcript: The same year Rothko made this, he opened a school. Thirty-five East Eighth Street. Him and a handful of other painters. John Cage even gave a lecture. So, put that aside for a second. Look at what Rothko is painting. A few years earlier, his pictures were packed. People. Plants. Little mythological guys everywhere. Here? Everybody got fired. No figures. No story. Pretty much nothing you can point at and name. Just thin washes soaking into the canvas. Green under blue. Orange coming through tan. Soft shapes hanging around. Which makes it look like Rothko is getting rid of the subject. He would absolutely disagree. Five years earlier, he and Adolph Gottlieb wrote this in the New York Times: "There is no such thing as a good painting about nothing." And then: "The subject is crucial." Okay. So where is it? That's the interesting part. Rothko isn't getting rid of the subject. He's getting rid of the stuff that does the explaining. No face telling you how somebody feels. No story telling you what happened. Whatever the subject is now, you're going to have to meet it some other way. And now, back to that school. It had a name. Subjects of the Artist. Of course it did. The school lasted less than a year. Rothko kept working on the subject for another twenty. In 1969, the year before he died, he gave this painting to MoMA. Himself.

title: NO. 5/NO. 24
transcript: Two numbers. No name. No. 5. Or No. 24. It's both. That barely counts as a title. Sounds like somebody was keeping track of boxes. Around this time, Rothko starts doing that a lot. The names disappear. He didn't like explaining what the paintings meant. And a title can do a lot of explaining before you've even looked. Call this Sunset and you're done. Orange, sky. Dark thing, horizon. Found it. Call it No. 5... nothing. No hint. No little story hiding in the title. So look. Brown across the middle. Black shapes. Pale color underneath. Orange pushing in around the edges. Your brain can turn those things into whatever it wants. Rothko just isn't helping. Which matters, because a Rothko didn't always look like this. You used to be able to take inventory. Recognize things. Count them. All gone. Now even the name won't give you anything to grab. No. 5. No. 24. Pick one. Either way, you're on your own.

title: ABRAHAM
transcript: It’s an almost-black painting with a black stripe running down it, just left of center. That’s pretty much it. Black on very dark brown. Nearly seven feet tall. People have looked at paintings like this and assumed they were unfinished. Or a prank. Or maybe the wall where the actual art was supposed to go. It’s none of those. Abraham was Newman’s father’s name. He’d died two years before this was painted. And then there’s the other Abraham. The Bible one. God tells him to take his son up a mountain and kill him, basically to prove he’s loyal. One of the most brutal tests of faith ever written. Now, it’s 1949. Four years after the war. Newman came out of it convinced the old ways of making pictures were finished. Beauty, harmony, the whole world-still-makes-sense routine. He wasn’t buying it anymore. Did he mean this painting as a picture of the camps? He never said that. But he doesn’t give you bodies. He doesn’t give you suffering. He gives you one dark vertical inside a dark field. Barely enough to say: something is standing here. Newman had destroyed almost everything he’d painted before this. Years of work. Gone. He said the old stuff wasn’t meaningful anymore. So he started again, basically from nothing, in his forties. And when he finally showed the new paintings, people treated them like an insult. He stopped showing for years. And people kept taking these paintings personally. In 1986, a guy named Gerard walked into the Stedelijk Museum in Amsterdam and slashed a Newman with a box cutter. Nearly fifty feet of cuts. Then eleven years later, Gerard came back looking for the same painting. Couldn’t find it. So he slashed a different Newman instead. Nobody does that to a painting they think is empty. And this one isn’t empty either. But it is holding something back. A father. A mountain. A silence with a name on it. Maybe. It’s under no obligation to hand any of that over.

title: UNTITLED
transcript: Your eyes are doing something a little embarrassing right now. They're trying to read this. They keep scanning left to right, row by row, like this is a page and sooner or later it's going to say something. It won't. But the painting knows that. Lee Krasner built it to do exactly this. The marks sit in rows. They line up like text. Little loops that feel almost like letters, shapes that feel like they might turn into numbers if you stare long enough. They never do. She called these the Little Image paintings. She made them between 1946 and 1950, working upstairs in a small bedroom in the Long Island house while Pollock had the barn. Some of them she called hieroglyphs, her word, because she wanted them to carry the pressure of writing even though there's no actual script here. And that part gets more interesting once you know Krasner grew up in an Orthodox Jewish household in Brooklyn and learned Hebrew as a child. That matters. Not because she's hiding Hebrew in the painting for you to decode. She isn't. It matters because she knew what it felt like to stand in front of dense, deliberate marks and have your whole body lean toward meaning. That's what this painting gives you. Rows. Rhythm. Repetition. Tiny variations that make you think, wait, was that one different? And then nothing resolves. No sentence forms. No word lands. You just stand there, wanting it to open, and it never does. It doesn't give you language. It gives you the urge for language, with nowhere to put it.

title: VIR HEROICUS SUBLIMIS
transcript: Damn! Look how big this thing is. Alright... now step a little closer. Closer than feels right. When Barnett Newman showed this in 1951, he put a note on the gallery wall. It basically said, people tend to look at big paintings from far away. Don't. This thing’s almost eight feet tall and eighteen feet wide. He wanted you to get close enough, so you can’t see where the red ends. Then you’ve got those lines. He called them zips. Strips of color running straight up and down. Some thin. Some wider. He compared standing in front of the painting to meeting another person. Except this one’s eighteen feet wide. A couple of years before, he’d written an essay called The Sublime Is Now. It basically said forget pretty. He wanted something that got to you. And he gives this painting a Latin title. Vir Heroicus Sublimis. Man, heroic and sublime. Now, don’t picture a guy on a horse. Think of yourself standing here. All that red in front of you. His first solo show had opened the year before. January 1950. The reviews were mostly hostile. Somebody even vandalized a painting right there in the gallery. He sold one. After the gallery took its cut, he was left with eighty-four dollars and fourteen cents. He was nearly forty-five. A year later, he comes back with this. And a note telling everybody to stand closer. That show goes badly too. Eight years before he gets another solo show in New York. Years later, MoMA wants to buy a group of paintings from a collector named Ben Heller. The trustees say yes to the Pollock. The Kline. The Gorky. This one, they won’t pay for. So Heller just gives it to them.

title: NUMBER 107
transcript: From across the room, it looks like someone primed the canvas and went to lunch. It's 1950, and New York painters are making a lot of noise. Pollock is flinging paint. De Kooning is beating the hell out of the canvas. Every brushstroke wants you to know who put it there. And Reinhardt paints white. Not one white. White over off-white, in short horizontal strokes stacked like brickwork. Nearly seven feet tall and barely three feet wide. A white column keeping very quiet and making you come to it. Here's what the calm hides. The guy was funny. Professionally funny. In 1946, Reinhardt drew cartoons about modern art for a New York newspaper called PM. In one of his best-known ones, a man points at an abstract painting, sneers, and asks, "What does this represent?" The painting grows arms, points back, and yells, "What do you represent?" That's Reinhardt in one gag. The painting doesn't owe you a picture. You owe it some attention. Four years later, he makes the same joke without the punch line. Nothing happens from across the room. Then you move closer. Rows appear. Whites separate. The surface starts shifting a little at a time. Everybody else was trying to knock you backward. Reinhardt made you lean forward. Then he kept going. Red paintings. Blue paintings. Then, around 1960, the black ones. Five feet square. A cross buried inside several blacks so close together your eyes need time to sort them out. He called them the last paintings anyone could make. When MoMA showed them, at least one member canceled in protest. A black square got somebody to quit the museum.

title: CHIEF
transcript: For years, Franz Kline was making these tiny little drawings. Phone book pages. Old envelopes. Scraps of paper. Chairs, streets, bridges. Stuff you could fold up and lose in your pocket. Then one night in 1948, he's hanging out in Willem de Kooning's studio. De Kooning has this projector in the corner. A Bell-Opticon. He grabs one of Kline's drawings. A black rocking chair, four inches by five. Let's see what happens. They turn off the lights and throw it up on the wall. And the thing goes huge. The legs of the chair stop looking like chair legs. Now they're girders. The little white gaps turn into windows. Suddenly it's a building you could walk into. Kline just stands there. Then he goes home and starts painting big. Five feet by six. Brushes as wide as your hand. Black paint flying across the canvas. At least, that's what it looks like. Like he walked up, took a few enormous swings, and went out for lunch. He didn't. Kline usually started with small drawings, then slowly rebuilt them on the canvas. Black, then white, then more black, then more white. The white isn't whatever he left blank. He painted that too. Kline said, "I paint the white as well as the black, and the white is just as important." Those narrow white lanes squeezing through the black. It's not black paint sitting on a white background. It's two paintings shoving each other around. Then there's the title. Chief. That was the name of a locomotive Kline remembered from growing up in Pennsylvania. His father killed himself when Kline was seven. A couple of years later he was sent away, to a school for fatherless boys. He came home at fifteen. By then his mother had married a foreman on the Lehigh Valley Railroad. So the tracks, the bridges, the trains, all that big black machinery, it was everywhere. It's what a train leaves behind after it tears past you.

title: ONE: NUMBER 31, 1950
transcript: Alright. Pick one of those looping lines, follow it for a second. Now picture Pollock making it. It's 1950, he's working in a barn in Springs out on Long Island. He's got the canvas spread across the floor, seventeen and a half feet of it. He's moving around it with a stick, paint running off the end. Sometimes it's one of those stiff, crusted brushes. Sometimes he just tips the can and pours. Most of the paint gets there through the air. Lands on the canvas. Supposedly there's even a fly caught in the black paint. It's a barn. You get flies. Anyway, follow that line again. Where it swings, where it thins out, where it changes direction. That's his arm moving. His wrist turning. His weight shifting as he reaches. That line you've been following is something he did. So the canvas isn't showing you what happened. It's where it happened. And that gives other painters a whole different idea of what the job could be. Willem de Kooning put it this way: "He busted our idea of a picture all to hell." He goes on to say there could be new paintings again. Anyway, Pollock was sober when he painted this. He'd stopped drinking in 1948, and some of the paintings that made him famous came out of those two years. The year before this one, Life magazine had asked if he was the greatest living painter in the United States. Then this photographer, Hans Namuth, comes out to photograph and film him working. You can still watch it. Pollock moving around the canvas, paint coming off the stick. Watch how carefully he places it. By the last filming session, they're outside. Pollock's painting on a sheet of glass with the camera underneath. You can watch the paint coming toward you. It's November. Cold. The story goes they come back into the house, and Pollock goes over to the sink, reaches down, pulls out a bottle of whiskey, pours himself a big glass, and tells Namuth, "This is the first drink I've had in two years."

title: WIRE SCULPTURES
transcript: She learned the technique in a market in Toluca, Mexico, in the summer of 1947. Not from an artist. From basket makers, women making functional objects out of looped wire, built to hold things. She watched, learned the basic loop, came back to Black Mountain College, and spent the next forty years finding out how much life one idea could hold. Then comes the familiar part: the art world spending years arguing about whether it counted as sculpture. Too repetitive. Too decorative. Too close to craft. Which, very often, was a polite way of saying: this looks like labor we already know how to undervalue. Because yes, she made them loop by loop, at a table in her house in San Francisco, with six children nearby, working for a while, stopping, then returning. And still the result is extraordinary. Each sculpture is made from a single continuous wire. One line, looped thousands of times into a form that holds other forms inside it: spheres inside lobes inside larger lobes, all of it visible at once. The inside and the outside exist at the same time. Nothing is hidden by the surface because the surface is mostly air. Asawa called it drawing in space. She's defining volume without filling it. Making something fully present without making it heavy. And the shadows matter too. When light passes through these forms, the shadow on the wall becomes as intricate as the sculpture itself. So the work doesn't just sit in the room. It echoes into it. Asawa once said she could "define the air without stealing it from anyone." What she saw in Toluca was a functional method. What she recognized in it was a whole new sculptural language. That's the leap. A technique for holding fruit becomes a way of holding space. And that's why these still feel so alive. Because they never quite pin space down. They just teach it how to stay visible. The fruit is long gone. These are still in the air.

title: SHE-GOAT
transcript: That belly was a wicker basket. Now it's the ribcage of a pregnant goat. So. South of France. Town full of potters. And the summer before, he'd won a goat in a lottery. Of course he did. A male goat. Then he decides to make one of his own. Next to his studio there's this yard full of broken ceramics, scrap metal, whatever the potters don't want. And Picasso starts shopping. Two ceramic jugs for the udders. Palm fronds for the back and that long goat face. Bits of metal wherever she looks like she might fall apart. Then he packs plaster around the whole mess. Okay. Now we got a goat. And all of it started in a trash pile. But here's the best part. There's a metal pipe where the butt goes. And at one point, inside the belly, there was this little rubber balloon. You squeezed the goat... noise came out the back. So, yeah. Picasso made a farting goat when he was pushing seventy. Then two years later, they cast her in bronze. Which is pretty great. The farting junk goat is now permanent. Heavy as hell. Museum piece. But get close. Jugs. Palm fronds. All those little scraps and textures are still right there.

title: NO. 5/NO. 22
transcript: By 1950, the rectangles are basically here. But this one still has a little scaffolding hanging around. Find the red band. Three skinny white lines run through it. They wobble. A few years from now, details like that are gone. Everything gets quieter. Right here, Rothko's still working it out. Now say something nice about the colors. Go ahead. Would've made him furious. In 1956, a writer named Selden Rodman gets Rothko talking. And Rothko tells him, flat out: I'm not an abstractionist. That he isn't interested in color for its own sake. He's interested in basic human emotions. Tragedy. Ecstasy. Doom. Not exactly paint-chip language. Then, two years later, Rothko actually writes down his recipe for a work of art. Seriously. Death. Sensuality. Tension. Irony. Wit and play. Chance. And then, at the bottom: "Hope. 10%." Ten percent. Apparently eleven would've been pushing it. That's Rothko. All this tragedy and doom, but wit is in there. Play is in there. Hope makes the list. And he thought the paintings actually worked. People cried in front of them. Rothko said those people were having the same religious experience he'd had while painting. He was completely sure something was getting across. How colored mud on a piece of cloth reaches into a stranger and turns something over... that part he couldn't explain. He just knew he'd watched it happen. So stop naming the colors for a second. See if anything happens.

title: NO. 10
transcript: So, look around. Rothko has somehow taken over the whole room. Most artists in this building get a wall. Maybe a corner. This guy gets the place to himself. He didn't call MoMA and demand it. But this is pretty close to how he wanted these paintings seen. Hang them low. Keep the light down. Don't let people stroll past, glance over, check Rothko off the list. He wanted you in there with them. Which is where you are. So you might as well use it. Get closer than feels polite. About eighteen inches. Now look at the yellow. Part of the trick is underneath. Under this entire painting is blue. He covered the whole canvas first with a thin wash of indigo. Then he started laying the other colors over it. White. Yellow. Cream. Thin enough that the earlier layers never completely shut up. Get close to the yellow and there's red underneath that too. At the edges, all these colors start leaking into each other's business. That's where a lot of the shimmer comes from. Nothing is just sitting on top. Now the other nice thing about this painting. It was the first Rothko ever to enter MoMA's collection. March 1952. Philip Johnson buys it from the Betty Parsons Gallery and hands it over. But the year before, curator Dorothy Miller had already spotted it while making the rounds of galleries. She's taking notes. And next to this painting she writes: Number ten. MMA? As in Museum of Modern Art. With a question mark.

title: 1951-T NO. 3
transcript: So. This is the third one. Not the third painting he made that year. The third time he made this painting. Nearly eight feet tall. Mostly black. Paint dragged down in long strokes, top to bottom, thick enough to leave ridges. Purple down the left side, with a stripe of blue in it. Bare canvas on the right. A white shape with a bite out of it. An orange one. And a streak of yellow way out at the edge. Then MoMA gets involved. In 1952, MoMA puts Clyfford in a group show. He only agrees because the curator, Dorothy Miller, gives his paintings a room of their own. The first version of this hangs in that room. This one doesn't exist yet. Two years later, the museum asks to buy it. But there's a small problem. By then, Still has destroyed it. He's already made a second one and sold that to a collector. So he paints MoMA a third. That's this. There's a fourth, too. That one he keeps. Across his career, he did this fifty-nine times. His explanation was simple. If the idea was good enough, it deserved more than one stretch of canvas. The man kept records. What he'd sold. What he'd lost. What he'd destroyed. And his own files describe this one as "deliberately inferior." "Hastily made." The one he sold to the Museum of Modern Art. Bottom left, down in the purple, he signed it. First name only. Clyfford. Fifty-one. Back when this one didn't exist.

title: BICYCLE WHEEL (THIRD VERSION, AFTER LOST ORIGINAL OF 1913)
transcript: So, originally, he didn't make this as a work of art. He made it because he liked watching the wheel spin. The story goes, Duchamp takes a bicycle wheel, turns it upside down, fastens it to a kitchen stool, and keeps it in his studio. Not for a museum. Not for a pedestal. Just to have around. He said it was like watching a fire in a fireplace. He'd give it a spin as he walked by. Nice thing to have in the room. Sure. Now look at what he actually built. A wheel that can't roll, because it's stuck on a stool. A stool you can't sit on, because there's a wheel in the way. Two completely useful things, joined together into one completely useless thing. And that uselessness, somehow, becomes enormous. People call this the first readymade. Or at least the first thing that later gets called a readymade. It's four years older than the famous urinal. So the most radical idea in twentieth-century art spends its first few years in a studio corner. Being a thing he liked. He hadn't noticed it was an idea yet. Then it gets better. He didn't protect it. Didn't preserve it. At some point, the studio gets cleared out, and the thing is gone. Lost. What you're looking at was made in 1951. Almost forty years later. The third version, after the original disappeared. And yes, he meant for the wheel to spin.

title: GOAT SKULL AND BOTTLE
transcript: He turns seventy this year. Decades of blowing art apart and putting it back together behind him. And now he’s down in the south of France making animals out of junk. The year before, Picasso built a whole goat. A big one. Pregnant. She’s downstairs in the sculpture garden. A year later, this. And, uh, the goat’s dead. Just the skull this time. Picasso built it out of whatever he could get his hands on. Bicycle handlebars for the horns. Two big bolt heads for the eyes. Corrugated cardboard for the fur. Nails for the scruff between the ears. And beside it, a bottle with a candle in the neck, more nails fanning out around the flame like rays of light. Now, a candle next to a skull is an old trick. Memento mori. Basically: time’s running out. You’re gonna die. So you’ve got Picasso building a skull out of trash and putting a candle beside it. Pretty dark. Except look at those horns. They’re still bicycle handlebars. You see both things at once. Goat. Bike. Skull. Pile of junk. And then, three years later, he makes it even stranger. He has the whole thing cast in bronze. The bolts. The nails. Even the cardboard. All of it. Bronze. Then he paints it gray. The same grim palette as his paintings during and just after the war. So he takes a pile of junk, turns it into bronze, then paints the bronze to look like junk again.

title: ECHO: NUMBER 25, 1951
transcript: So... Jackson Pollock bought turkey basters by the dozen. That's according to his wife, Lee Krasner. Ya know, the kitchen kind. But first, it's 1951, and the drip paintings have made him famous. Canvas on the floor. Paint poured and dripped into those enormous tangles of lines. That March, they're in Vogue. Cecil Beaton photographed models in ball gowns standing in front of them. And just as people are getting used to what a Pollock looks like, he starts making these. Black enamel on bare canvas. Whole stretches of cloth left showing. This is Echo. Krasner said he handled those things like a giant fountain pen. He had to control how much paint came out while moving his hand. So he's basically drawing. With something you'd normally use to make dinner. And look what's turning up. Upper left. That big eye. Little strokes across the top, like lashes. By June, he's writing to his painter friend Alfonso, saying some of his old images are coming through. He thinks this will bother two groups of people. Ya know, the crowd who thought the whole point was you weren't supposed to recognize anything. And then "the kids who think it simple to splash a Pollock out." He shows the black paintings that November. Some of the people who'd come around to the drips now have a whole new Pollock to deal with. But Krasner knew something they didn't. She'd watched his paintings being made. A lot of them, she said, had started with things you could recognize. Heads. Parts of bodies. Creatures. Then he'd keep working, and they'd disappear into the paint. She asked him once why he didn't stop while you could still make out what was there. "I choose to veil the imagery," he said. Cover it up, basically. But with these, she said, he mostly left it showing. Why? She didn't know. Wasn't sure he could've told you either.

title: NUMBER 3 (UNTITLED)
transcript: Alright so, Lee Krasner finally gets a show of her own. She's been painting for twenty-five years. Fall of 1951. Betty Parsons Gallery in New York. Fourteen paintings. One reviewer says it's like traveling through a vast uninhabited land of quiet color. Sounds promising, right? Nothing sells. This is one of the fourteen. Look at the dark red stripe, just left of the middle. The widest one. Even there, the paint's thin enough for the canvas to show through. Then there's that little hairline of yellow, about halfway down, just right of the middle. Barely anything. And over on the left, a skinny red stripe keeps breaking off and starting again. A couple of years later, Krasner's got her studio covered in black-and-white drawings. Floor to ceiling, all the way around. One day she walks in and hates all of it. Takes them down. Rips them apart. Throws them on the floor. She said later, "I don't know why I did it, except I certainly did it." So... she just leaves them there. Doesn't go back for a couple of weeks. Usually, when you leave a mess for two weeks, what you come back to is a mess. But she starts looking at the pieces. Something about them interests her. She picks them up and starts making collages. Then she goes after some of her oil paintings. Cuts those up too. By 1955, she has another show. Big collages. Torn edges, black patches, pieces of painted canvas put together in new ways. That's her turning point. And underneath some of them? The paintings from that first show. The ones nobody bought. Some became scraps. Others became the surface she built on. Only two survive as they were. You're looking at one.

title: THE SWIMMING POOL
transcript: He's eighty-two. In a wheelchair. Matisse tells Lydia, his assistant, that he wants to see some divers. So they go to a swimming pool in Cannes. The sun's blazing. He can't take it. They go home. And Matisse announces, dead serious: "I will make myself my own pool." So, he gets out the scissors. He cuts swimmers, divers, and sea creatures out of paper painted blue. His assistants pin them against a long white strip running around his dining room. Almost fifty-four feet of it. He can sit down to dinner with somebody diving over his head. He called it drawing with scissors. And for the last two years of his life, he lives with this pool going around him. After he dies, it has to come off the walls. His wife and daughter want it to keep looking like that room. The walls had been covered in burlap. So they have the paper mounted on new burlap. They know burlap is bad for paper. They do it anyway. Then the burlap goes brown. Its acid starts staining the paper. In 1993, MoMA takes it down. Twenty years off the wall. The old burlap is stuck to the paper. In places, they have to take it off one thread at a time. And when the swimmers go back up, nobody glues them down. They use pins. Through the same little holes his assistants made in Matisse's dining room.

title: THE DEVIL WITH CLAWS
transcript: Follow the wire. It runs from the creature's hand, through the open space of its body, down to its foot. There's one on the other side, too. Actual wire. Pulled tight. You'll miss it for a second. Then you can't unsee it. This is Germaine Richier. 1952. And right around now she starts doing this thing: running wire through her sculptures. Before this, her figures stood the way sculpture is supposed to stand. On their own. Then suddenly the body is caught inside these lines. OK. First read: trap. Cage. Something holding the figure in place. But look again. Those lines also look like plumb lines, the tool sculptors use to check if a figure is hanging straight. So the thing trapping the body is also the thing measuring it. That's very Richier. Now look at the creature itself. Pointed head. Spider hands. Bent body. Reaching two ways at once. You honestly can't tell if it's pulling against the wires or hanging from them. Probably both. And she knew this stuff from the inside. She trained with Bourdelle, who'd worked for Rodin. She could make a textbook bronze in her sleep. The proper upright body, standing nicely on a pedestal. But this is 1952. Postwar. A proper standing body wasn't enough anymore. So she makes this. Half-human, half-creature, rough all over, standing on a block that feels less like a pedestal and more like a piece of ground. She once said her bronzes were like ancient figures pulled out of the sea. Bodies that had already been through something before you ever got to see them. That's exactly what this feels like. Not broken. Not whole. More like a body that survived one disaster and got caught in something else right after. She took the old tools, bronze, balance, the upright figure, and used them to make something that looks measured and trapped at the same time. She didn't abandon sculpture. She made it nervous.

title: WOMAN, II
transcript: Look at that smile. Just above the lips. See that straight edge? Sorta looks like he cut the mouth out of something and stuck it on. It's paint. But on the first painting in this series, de Kooning actually did use mouths cut from magazines. Advertising smiles. He said it helped to have something real there. This is Woman Two. The first one took him nearly two years. Paint her in. Scrape whole sections off. Paint her in again. Try following one of her arms. There's an outline, then it just kinda disappears into the paint. Drips run down her chest. And this guy could draw. Years of academy training in Rotterdam. So... getting a woman onto the canvas wasn't the problem. Leaving her alone was. At one point he took the first painting off the stretcher and gave up. A friend encouraged him to go back to it. So back she went. Which makes you wonder: how the hell does he know when it's finished? Years later, somebody actually asked him. He said simply: "I just stop." Alright, well... that clears that up. Anyway, this one he painted in the summer of 1952, on an art dealer's porch in East Hampton. Leo Castelli's. So... in 1953, he shows six of the women together. By now, he's made his name painting things that don't look like things. And here he is painting women again. Some of the other painters took that personally. At the after party, Jackson Pollock reportedly tells him, "Bill, you betrayed it. You're doing the figure, you're still doing the same goddamn thing." So... apparently, there were rules. Other people saw the paintings as violent, misogynistic. Anyway, when MoMA bought the first one, their own committee found it "quite frightening." But... they also liked the color.

title: SACKCLOTH 1953
transcript: So this is the guy who got the Italian parliament asking questions about a sack. We’ll get there. Start with that long white thread up top. It comes loose from a patch and wanders off to the left across the burlap. Alberto Burri. Before he’s an artist, he’s a doctor in the Italian army. During the Second World War, the British capture him in Tunisia. He ends up in a prisoner-of-war camp in Texas. They won’t let him practice medicine, so he starts painting. Art supplies run short, and he starts using empty burlap sacks from the mess hall. Paints on those. He later says, “I painted every day. It was a way of not having to think about the war and everything around me.” After the war, they send him home, and he gives up medicine for good. A few years later, he’s using sacks again. But now he’s cutting them up and sewing them together on a canvas. Look at the patches. The frayed one near the top. The gray one stitched on below it. The cloth gives him color. The stitching gives him lines. Even the holes become part of the picture. He’s making a painting out of the sack itself. So, a doctor, sewing up torn cloth. You can see where people go with that. The guy running the Guggenheim calls him an artist with a scalpel. When Burri tries to explain his own painting, he says, “Words are no help to me.” And then there are the people who can’t get past the sack. What’s an old sack doing on a museum wall? In Rome, the national modern art gallery hangs a big one of these sack paintings. The argument makes it all the way to parliament. A senator raises questions about the work. Another politician wants the woman running the museum moved to a different job. Over a sack. By then, MoMA had already bought this one. The year he makes this, an American artist, Robert Rauschenberg, visits his studio in Rome. Two years later, Rauschenberg’s putting a quilt in a painting. Burri keeps going too. Burns wood. Melts plastic. Welds sheets of metal. So go back to those holes. You can see the dark canvas behind them. In Texas, he used sacks because he needed something to paint on. Here, he’s got canvas. And he’s put the sacks on top of it.

title: FLAG
transcript: Before Jasper Johns paints this, he destroys almost everything he's made. He's twenty-four. And the way he later tells it, he's had enough of trying to become an artist. Time to actually be one. Then he has a dream that he's painting a big American flag. The next morning, he goes out and buys the materials. Starts with a bedsheet and house paint. Except the paint takes too long to dry. He wants to put down a stroke and have it stay there while he does the next one. So he tries hot wax with the color mixed in. Encaustic, it's called. Sets as it cools. So, now he can keep going. Get closer to it. Those stripes are built out of newspaper and bits of cloth, dipped in wax and laid inside pencil lines. You can still read pieces of the paper through the paint. From across the room, an American flag. Up here, he's practically built the thing scrap by scrap. And choosing a flag took one job off his hands. He didn't have to design it. The stars go here. The stripes go there. That part's settled. Now he can get on with making the painting. He called these "things the mind already knows." He'd go on to paint targets. Numbers. Maps. At a time when the big New York painters are making enormous abstract things, Johns starts with something every kid in school could draw. But an American flag comes with a little more baggage than a set of stripes. He starts this in 1954. The year "under God" goes into the Pledge. The year the Senate censures Joe McCarthy. And here's Johns, painting the flag on a bedsheet. Is it a flag? Is it a picture of a flag? People have been arguing about that since the sixties. January 1958. His first solo show, at Leo Castelli's gallery. Alfred Barr, who helped start this museum, wants four paintings. He gets three. This is the one they get stuck on. The people approving the purchase worry it could look unpatriotic. So Barr finds a way around them. Barr gets his architect buddy to buy it, with the idea that he'll give it to the museum later. Later turns out to be fifteen years. Finally Philip Johnson gives it to MoMA. In Barr's honor. And underneath all that trouble, the newspaper's still in there. Stock reports. Ads. A Hollywood figure telling you how to lose weight. And a recipe for applesauce.

title: EAMES LOUNGE CHAIR
transcript: This chair went on television before it went anywhere else. 1956. NBC. A daytime show called Home, hosted by Arlene Francis. The chair comes out in silhouette first, like a mystery guest. Then the lights come up. Charles Eames stands beside it, listing the ingredients like he's describing a sandwich. Rosewood. Plywood. Leather. "Its insides are all feathers and down." Then they run a little stop-motion film where the chair builds itself, takes itself apart, and climbs into a Herman Miller shipping box. Francis looks at it and says, "Well, that is quite a departure, Charles." She wasn't kidding. The Eameses were known for chairs you could make a lot of. Molded plywood. Fiberglass. Stack them up, send them out, let everybody have one. And then this thing arrives. Expensive. One chair for one person, and that person is doing all right. But it leans back with you. It gives a little. Charles said he wanted it to have the warm, receptive look of a well-used first baseman's mitt. Which is a lot to ask from rosewood and leather. But look at it. He got pretty close. A lot of expensive chairs seem designed for somebody else to see you sitting in them. This one is for what happens after they leave. The cheaper Eames chairs came and went. Some disappeared from the catalog for decades before being brought back. The departure never left. People got a little bigger, though. About an inch taller, on average, since 1956. So eventually Herman Miller made a taller one.

title: BRAUN SK4 RECORD PLAYER
transcript: In 1956, a record player was furniture. A big wooden cabinet with the machine shut away inside it, like something you shouldn't look at. Then Braun put out this. A pale metal box, wooden sides, and a lid you can see straight through. Hans Gugelot and Dieter Rams designed it, back when everything electric was trying to look expensive. Big dials. Heavy cabinets. Weighed a ton, so you'd know it was serious. They went the other way. Buttons that look like buttons. Knobs that behave like knobs. Nothing showing off. Rams spent the rest of his career turning that into rules. Good design is honest. Good design is unobtrusive. Good design is as little design as possible. Half the things in your pocket still run on those sentences. Now. The lid. The first plan was sheet metal. Then the engineers switched the speaker on. The lid rattled. So they swapped it for plastic. Gugelot thought the stuff was a fad. The name that stuck was Snow White's Coffin. Two years later, MoMA took one. The coffin outlived the furniture.

title: THE JUGGLER (THE MAGICIAN)
transcript: Alright, so, Remedios Varo wrote notes about her own paintings. In the note for this one, she says the guy in the hat… “is full of tricks.” Then she gives you a little tour. So… might as well take it. He’s got all his tools around him on his cart. And the animals stand for the four elements. There’s an owl on the chair. A goat in the window. A lion on the floor. Doves up on the roof. You can probably guess which one’s fire. The green bottles are potions. And there are dried herbs by the flask. Okay, now look at his face. The hat on top, the beard below. Together, they make a five-pointed star. And the face itself is painted on a sliver of mother-of-pearl. About a millimeter thick, set into the board. She did that in only five paintings. Then there’s the crowd. She says one cloak joins them all. Twenty-one people in one piece of gray cloth. Same hair, too. Now, one to find on your own. Look at the window next to the goat. There’s a woman in blue, eyes closed. Some people have wondered if that’s Varo herself. She painted this in Mexico City. Civil war got her out of Spain. The Germans got her out of Paris, where she’d been running with the Surrealists. A boat got her the rest of the way. In Mexico, she fixed old pottery for money. Didn’t start painting full-time until her mid-forties. And around the time she painted this, she had her first solo show. Crowds came. There was a waiting list. Check the crowd’s eyes. Some are on him. Some are on you.

title: PAINTING
transcript: When Pierre Soulages was a kid, he was drawing black lines on white paper. A friend of his sister's asked what he was making. A snow scene, he said. With black ink. Years later, he thought he understood it: the black had made the white paper look brighter. Now look toward the lower left. Those little streaks of olive and gold. Against this much black, a little goes a long way. And those big black strokes overlap almost like boards in a pile. Little lines around the edges keep them from becoming one solid lump. Soulages even made tools from rubber meant for the bottoms of shoes. Spread the paint, drag it, scrape it back. This is called Painting. August 1, 1956. But stay with those little flashes of gold. Then, in 1979, he's in the studio, working on another painting. Black everywhere. Hours of work. He thinks it's going badly. Exhausted, he goes to sleep for an hour. Comes back. The painting hasn't changed. But what he sees has. Now he notices the light coming off the black. As he later put it: "I don't paint with black anymore. I paint with the light reflected off the black surface."

title: JACOB'S LADDER
transcript: A guy named Jacob falls asleep on the ground with a rock for a pillow. His brother wants him dead. Jacob had tricked their father into giving him the blessing meant for his brother. Alright, so we got some family trouble. Then he dreams a ladder going from the dirt all the way to heaven. Angels up and down it like a fire escape. He wakes up and says, more or less, God was here and I had no idea. That's the story behind the title of this painting. Jacob's Ladder. Although there's no sleeping guy in it. No little angels. So how did Helen Frankenthaler get there? New York painting in the fifties is a boys' club. Pollock has put his canvas on the floor and dripped paint across it. Helen likes the floor too. At twenty-three, she lays down a raw canvas, thins her oil paint, and pours. The paint sinks into the cloth. The next spring, a critic with a lot of pull brings two painters over to see what she's done. They go home and start pouring too. Five years after that first pour, she makes this one. Same move. The pouring move that made her name. Nine and a half feet tall. Rust red. Pale green. Lavender. Pink. Plenty of canvas left bare. Up top, a big pink burst, marks flung out like fingers. Down near the bottom, a patch of blue with short strokes laid across it. Rungs, once you see them. Years earlier, she had seen an old painting of Jacob's dream in Madrid. In that one, the ladder isn't made of wood. It's made of light. But she said the ladder in this painting showed up bit by bit while she worked. The shapes started to suggest an "exuberant figure and ladder. Therefore Jacob's Ladder." Her words. Including the "therefore."

title: SKY CATHEDRAL
transcript: Okay, so it’s the middle of the night in Kips Bay, Manhattan. A woman pushing sixty is going through what the neighbors left on the curb. Her block’s being torn down, so the sidewalk’s basically… a free yard sale. Chair legs. Banisters. Lettuce crates. Milk boxes. Spindles. She hauls it all home. Her name is Louise Nevelson. So… for years, she and her son picked up wood off the street to burn in the fireplace. Some of that wood still had nails in it. Nail holes, too. So she stopped burning it and just nailed it all together. And she knew. This was art. Then she did what any decent thief does with the score. Painted it all one color. Flat black. Her first wall. Nearly sixty boxes, stacked over eleven feet high. She calls it Sky Cathedral. Have a look. A chair leg and a stair rail and a crate slat are the same stuff now. You couldn’t pick your own furniture out of this lineup. She said she hadn’t chosen black. “It chose me.” So… when she first showed this, the gallery walls were painted dark, and the lights were turned down to a dim blue, and people kept bumping into things. A critic called her sculptures “appalling and marvelous.” Even Life magazine ran a story. Now, the museum wanted the wall. But it didn’t have the money to buy it. So it came in as a gift from Mr. and Mrs. Ben Mildwoff. Who are they? Turns out Mrs. Mildwoff was her… sister.

title: GUANO-ROUND
transcript: Alright. The title’s Guano-Round. Guano is bird shit. The stuff that piles up on islands, layer after layer. Now look at that big gray circle. All crusted over, with these little pits in it. Looks like it’s been sitting out in the weather for a thousand years. And down at the bottom, that little red drip running onto the white. Her name’s Judit Reigl. She’s in Hungary after the war, getting commissions to paint Stalin and the party bosses. She wants to get to Paris. They won’t give her a passport. Won’t even give her paint. So she tries to leave anyway. Eight attempts. Doesn’t make it. The ninth time, in 1950, she gets across the border. Then she’s walking, hitching rides, making her way across Europe to Paris. André Breton, the man running the Surrealists, likes her work. Gives her a show. She joins the group, but she doesn’t stay. She says later that she’d left one bloc so as not to belong to another. Anyway, she’s got these paintings that haven’t worked out. She’s given up on them, but she’s kept the canvases. Then she gets a new wooden floor in her studio and needs something to protect it. So those old paintings go down on the floor, this one included. And she keeps making other paintings. Paint lands on the canvases under her feet, soaks in, dries. She walks over them while she works. This goes on for years. She calls them “excremental rags.” Her words. All those layers building up like the bird shit. So that crust you’re looking at. That’s what happened under her feet. Eventually, she goes back to those canvases. The pictures she’d rejected have disappeared under all this paint. But now there’s something else she can work with. She takes a tool she’s made herself and starts scraping into it. Even the last coat of paint, usually white, goes on and then gets scraped right back off. Some stays behind over the older layers. So look at that circle again. Paint had been building up on this thing for years. And then she starts making a new picture by taking some of it away. She calls it “a backwards operation.”

title: NO. 37/NO. 19 (SLATE BLUE AND BROWN ON PLUM)
transcript: Looks like somebody turned the lights down on this one. Plum. Slate blue. This big heavy bar of brown. On the other wall in this room you've got yellow, orange, red. Same basic setup. Completely different mood. And in 1958, Rothko lands the biggest commission of his life. The Four Seasons. Brand-new restaurant inside the Seagram Building. Bronze. Money. Very expensive lunch. They offer him thirty-five thousand dollars to paint the dining room. He says yes. Then he makes more than thirty paintings for a room that only needs about seven. Because Rothko isn't really thinking about decoration anymore. He wants the paintings to take over the room. A place, he called it. Not a bunch of pictures hung around a restaurant. And the place he has in mind is not relaxing. He loved this room by Michelangelo in Florence where the windows feel blocked and the walls close in. Rothko said it made you feel trapped. That's what he wanted. Then, on a boat to Europe, he tells the writer John Fischer the other part. He wants to ruin the appetite of every son of a bitch who eats in that room. His words. So. Restaurant decoration. Not really. Then Rothko and his wife finally go eat at the Four Seasons. He sees the room. Sees the people. Sees the whole expensive machine of it. And pulls out. Gives the money back. Keeps the paintings. This canvas isn't one of the murals. It's just what Rothko's hand was doing that same year. Going dark. Going heavy. And the murals themselves? Nobody ever ate a meal under them.

title: CANYON
transcript: This painting cannot be sold. Federal law. That eagle's the problem. 1959. Robert Rauschenberg gets a phone call from his friend Sari. She lives above Carnegie Hall. And the way he tells it, her neighbor's just died. One of the last of Teddy Roosevelt's Rough Riders. The janitors have pushed his belongings into the hallway. Among them, a stuffed eagle. Does he want it? Alright, so... Rauschenberg's already the guy people offer this stuff to. He's been putting real things into paintings. A quilt. A tire. A stuffed goat. People keep asking whether they're paintings or sculptures. His son says he made up a word to scare them off. Combines. So the eagle goes back to his studio. He cuts off its tail so it'll fit against the canvas. Wings out. That open cardboard box underneath it. Below that, a pillow hanging from a string. Tied around the middle. Like a butt. And up on the left, in the black frame, that's his son, Christopher. A baby reaching up. He calls it Canyon. An art dealer, Ileana Sonnabend, buys it. Keeps it for decades. Then the eagle becomes a problem. Federal laws protect these birds. Dead ones, too. You can't just sell one because you've put it in a painting. Rauschenberg has to send a notarized statement saying the bird was killed before 1940. After that, Sonnabend can keep it. Selling it is still out. Then she dies in 2007, and her children inherit it. The appraisers have to put a number on it for the estate. Can't legally sell it. They put down zero. The IRS comes back with sixty-five million. Same painting. And a bill for about forty-one million in taxes and penalties. Now, according to the family's lawyer, an IRS official suggested there might be a buyer after all. Some billionaire in China. Willing to buy it and hide it. So the family's supposed to pay tax on a sale they're not allowed to make. Their lawyer puts it this way: sell it to pay the tax, and you go to jail. Eventually, they make a deal. The family gives Canyon to a museum. The IRS drops the tax claim. The family gets no tax deduction for the gift. In 2012, it comes here. Rauschenberg had a simpler explanation for why he used stuffed animals. He wanted to give them another life. He said, "I always thought, it's too bad they're dead." And then: "I thought I can do something about that."

title: UNTITLED
transcript: Look at the hole. Not the whole thing. The hole. That black opening in the center. Your eye already went there before you even meant it to. And that's the trick. That darkness isn't painted on. It's real depth. An actual cavity in the relief, dropping back behind the surface. You can't see the end of it from here. Your eye goes in and just stays there. Everything around it is built from salvage. Welded steel underneath. Canvas stretched over it, but not nice painting canvas. Laundry bags. Tarps. Industrial material. The kind of fabric made to carry things, catch things, get dirty, get used up. She went to industrial suppliers for this stuff. Which is part of why the thing feels so strange. It looks a little like a jet intake. A little like a mouth. A little like an organism nobody's named yet. She made dozens of these in the late 1950s and 60s, and she called every one of them Untitled. Every one. That was deliberate. She wasn't going to rescue you with a title. Wasn't going to say: here, this is a flower, this is a body, this is grief, this is landscape. You had to stand there and deal with the thing itself. Then in the early 1970s, she stopped. Not because the work had failed. It hadn't. She was known. Collected. In the conversation. She just walked away, moved to a farm in Pennsylvania, and spent years making things out of public view. And when she came back in the 1990s, the work still had the same force. That center still pulls. Still withholds. Still refuses to tell you what you're looking at. She never explained it. She made sure the hole got there first.

title: COCOON NO. 2
transcript: Stand right in front of this one. Looks flat, right? Small diamond. Black, cream. A painting. Now move over a little. There. The black part folds out from the wall. And behind it, this little pocket of dark. So the painting has an inside now. The year Lygia Clark made this, 1959, she wrote a letter to Mondrian. Piet Mondrian. Grids. Primary colors. Very flat. One problem. He'd been dead for fifteen years. She writes him anyway. "If I work, Mondrian..." She's talking to the dead guy directly. And then, basically, tells him there's more to it than making surfaces. Which is a pretty good letter to send the guy who spent his life perfecting the surface. Clark had been making geometric paintings too. Then she and a group of Brazilian artists started calling themselves the Neo-Concretists. Translated from art manifesto: Geometry had gotten way too good at behaving itself. Too clean. Too rational. Too much like math homework. They wanted it to act more like a thing. Something with a body. Something you had to deal with. And Clark starts here. Sheet metal. Painted like a picture. Hung like a picture. Then she folds one part out. That's it. Tiny move. But now there's a front, a side, an inside. She called these Cocoons. Which fits. A cocoon isn't really the finished thing. It's the thing while it's becoming something else. And that's basically what this is. Not quite a painting anymore. Not quite the sculptures Clark is about to start making either. After this, her work keeps coming farther off the wall until eventually you're supposed to pick it up. But here's the first move. And there's a Mondrian hanging in this room. Which is nice.

title: SPATIAL CONCEPT: EXPECTATION
transcript: So. Fontana said this. "I pierce this canvas that was the basis of all art, and I have created an infinite dimension." Okay. It's a brown canvas with one cut in it. So what the hell is he talking about? Well, Fontana thought painting was basically finished. He'd already tried leaving it behind. Nine years before the first cut, he blacked out a gallery in Milan. Hung a fluorescent paper-mâché shape from the ceiling. Turned on ultraviolet lights. You didn't stand in front of it. You walked into it. Six days later, it was gone. That's what he was after. Light. Color. The room itself. The cut is him trying to make a canvas do the same thing. Fontana started as a sculptor. He'd been one for more than thirty years before the first cut. He started in his father's shop in Argentina, making monuments for cemeteries. Tombstones. Angels. A sculptor doesn't fake a back. He makes one. So when Fontana comes back to the canvas, he doesn't fake it in paint. He pulls a blade through it. And he gets one shot. If the cut goes wrong, there's no painting over it. The whole canvas goes. "You have no idea how much stuff I throw away," he said. Now get close. This one landed. It isn't some wild slash. He works the opening with his hands. Wide through the middle. Pointed at either end. The edges turned slightly inward. And now there really is space behind the painting. Done. Except then he covers it up. Black gauze, glued across the back. That's the darkness in the cut. Not the room. Not infinity. Fabric. Without the gauze, the cut ends at the wall. With it, it keeps going. Fontana had a name for that black cloth. The teletta. The little canvas. So, to get beyond the canvas, Fontana cut through one. Then put another one behind it.

title: FRAGMENT FROM HOMAGE TO NEW YORK
transcript: The sculpture garden, downstairs. A Thursday evening, March 1960. Half past six. In the middle of the garden is a machine the size of a two-story house. Painted white. All of it. A couple hundred people stand around it. Ya know, invited. Good clothes. So the fall before, Jean Tinguely put a hundred fifty thousand copies of a manifesto out in Düsseldorf. Story goes, out of a plane. The gist was simple. Nothing holds still. So quit pretending anything lasts. Then he comes to New York and builds something that won't last through dinner. He does it with Billy Klüver, an engineer at Bell Labs. They drag the materials back from dumps, scrapyards and junk shops. A player piano. A radio. A bathtub. A bassinet. A toilet. Bicycle wheels. An American flag. The whole thing is built to destroy itself. So, it starts up. Wheels turning. Metal on metal. The piano banging away. A weather balloon fills up, keeps filling, then pops. Colored smoke pours out. The machine paints a picture and tears it up. Then it paints another one. Bottles come down and smash. Sparks fly. Then flames. NBC is filming. A piece breaks off and hits one of their camera crew. That's when a New York City fireman steps forward and puts it out. It's not even seven. The machine wasn't finished destroying itself. Twenty-seven feet high that night. What's left is six foot eight. White metal. Bicycle wheels. A paint can with a red band. A big wooden disc down low, like the end of a cable spool. That long curved rod over everything. And up top, a little red flag in rags. The original machine was called Homage to New York. This is Fragment from Homage to New York. Honest, at least. That night, people went through the wreckage and took parts home. Souvenirs. Not this one. This one turns up in the collection eight years later. Gift of the artist.

title: KICHKA'S BREAKFAST I
transcript: So this is the guy who glued his girlfriend’s breakfast down and hung it on the wall. Daniel Spoerri. And look at what it’s sitting on. A kitchen chair, with a board across the seat. So, start on the right. A tin of salt. A can of Nescafé. Then a glass, an opened can of condensed milk, the coffeepot. Two white bowls. Keep going. That red eggcup. Look close. The shell’s still in it. And at the far left, a little tin lid full of cigarette butts. Coffee. Egg. Cigarette. Maybe that’s how the morning went. It’s 1960. Spoerri’s living in a hotel room in Paris. His girlfriend, Kichka, has finished breakfast. He’s waiting for visitors, and all this is still sitting there. His words: “I pasted together the morning’s breakfast, which was still there by chance.” Then he hangs it on the wall. Chair and all. This is the first of what he calls snare pictures. Traps. He takes things where he finds them, fixes them in place, and turns the whole thing upright. The board that was lying flat is now facing you. So, if a painting of breakfast is a picture of a morning, this is the morning. MoMA buys this one the next year. And then he keeps going. In 1963, he turns a Paris gallery into a restaurant. He cooks. Art critics wait the tables. And when the meal’s over, the dishes and leftovers get fixed in place. The table goes up on the wall. So go back to that little lid. “Still there by chance.” That’s how he found the breakfast. Those cigarette butts are still there now, because he glued them down.

title: GRANDES CARRIÈRES
transcript: All right, it’s nine in the morning in New York, and Joan Mitchell’s out walking her dog. She runs into Hans Hofmann, one of the big painters in town. He goes, “Mitchell, you should be painting.” She remembered him as very supportive. “Very nice,” she said. Then she goes on: “I don’t think women in any way were a threat to these men, so they could encourage the ‘lady painter.’” At this point she’s already showing alongside Pollock and de Kooning. But the history books have a little name for her, too. Second-generation Abstract Expressionist. Basically, the younger crowd making those big, splashy paintings. She had a word for that, too. Boring. “We were painting at the same time as they were,” she said. So at this point, New York is the center of this whole thing. Her friends are there. Her career’s there. She’s in the room. And she just gets up and leaves. For Paris. She doesn’t know anybody. She doesn’t even speak French. Anyways, a couple of years later, she makes this. It’s nearly ten feet across. Look at that dark thing in the middle. Brown and blue, all jammed together. Then the pinks, and splatters of green and teal breaking off around it. Even that pale stuff around the edges is full of little lines and smears of color. Kinda feels like you’ve just missed the whole thing happening. But she could spend weeks on a painting. Sometimes months. She’s working from memory. Somewhere she’s been, the feeling it left behind. And she’s looking for the point where the paint starts giving her that feeling back. “The freedom in my work is quite controlled,” she said. “I don’t close my eyes and hope for the best.” So, eventually, she’s got the painting. Then it gets a name. This is Grandes Carrières. Big quarries. A neighborhood in Paris.

title: BLUE MONOCHROME
transcript: Okay. Just stand here a second. Obviously, it’s blue. But notice how it’s not shiny. Not really smooth either. Kinda powdery. The guy is Yves Klein. French. From Nice. This one’s from ’61. Alright, so at nineteen, this guy’s lying on the beach in Nice. Looks up at the blue sky. And signs it. In his imagination. Calls that his first artwork. Then gets annoyed with the birds. Says they’re making holes in it. So that’s who we’re dealing with. Anyway, getting that blue onto a board takes some work. It’s ultramarine. A pigment painters have used for centuries. It’s beautiful as powder. But when you mix it with oil, the life of the color just kinda… comes out of it. Klein wants the powder to stay looking like powder. So he goes to a paint shop in Montparnasse. Works with a guy named Édouard Adam.
