Lovers. Old people. Lives from all over the world. The idea is that we all belong to one human family. It sells millions. That money buys MoMA photographs for years. Including this one. Okay, look past them at the river. Baltrop photographed bodies pulled out of that water, too. Cops standing around them. He said he wanted to save “the frightening, mad, unbelievable, violent, and beautiful things” going on out there.

title: UNTITLED FILM STILLS
transcript: These movies don't exist. That's the first thing. Your brain keeps trying to remember the title. Was this Hitchcock? Something Italian, maybe. Black-and-white, emotionally devastating, nobody says what they mean. Nope. Fake. All of it. In 1977, Cindy Sherman was twenty-three and new to New York, answering phones at a downtown gallery called Artists Space. The first six of these were shot at home, in the apartment she shared with the artist Robert Longo. Six photos. One imaginary blonde actress, caught at different points in a career that never existed. Wigs, cheap jackets, a tripod. Sherman handled the costume, lighting, pose, expression, then stepped into the frame. She was the actress, the director, the costume department, hair and makeup. The whole studio, except for the movie. And you know these women instantly. The hitchhiker. The secretary. The woman who just realized she trusted the wrong man forty-five seconds too late. Which is disturbing, because you've never met her. You've met the template. They look exactly like promotional stills. Not the movie, the advertisement for the movie. She printed them at about eight by ten inches, the size of a real studio glossy. Except there's no story. Just the suggestion of one. Your brain finishes it. You write the plot. You invent the danger. You supply the emotional damage. She stopped after three years. Sixty-nine photographs, then out. Didn't run it into the ground. In December 1995, MoMA bought the complete set. At the time, its film archive already held four million real studio stills. Four million photographs from movies that exist. And sixty-nine from movies that don't.

title: FIRST REQUIEM
transcript: Anne Truitt takes three baths that night. Still can't sleep. She's sitting in the middle of the bed, she later writes, "like a frog on a lily pad." All because of an afternoon looking at art. November 1961. She's forty, living in Washington, visiting New York with a friend. They go to the Guggenheim. Down near the bottom of the ramp, she comes around a corner and sees a painting by Barnett Newman. A great stretch of blue. And the word she remembers is "enough." Enough space. Enough color. She hadn't known a painting could give her that. Back in Washington, she goes to the lumber store. Orders some boards. Buys glue, clamps, white house paint. Puts together something that looks like a piece of picket fence. Calls it First. Soon she's making painted wooden boxes. By 1963, she's got a show in New York. Donald Judd, a sculptor who also writes reviews, pans it. A few years later, a critic says she beat the Minimalists to it. If only she'd painted each piece one color. Judd's reply: "If the queen had balls, she would be king." Truitt, meanwhile, is putting up to forty coats of paint on these things. Herself. Sanding between layers. A workshop builds the wooden shapes from her drawings. The surface is her job. All that work, and you can barely see how it was done. Now look at this one. First Requiem. 1977. Eight inches across. More than seven feet tall. Pink. Yellow. Dark red. Black. From here, maybe a very tall paint sample. But walk around it. The sides don't match. There's turquoise you couldn't see before. And down at the bottom, the base is tucked underneath. The column stops just short of the floor. She's worked out how it meets the room, right down to that little gap. Then there's the title. First Requiem. A requiem is music for the dead. Years later, she explained what had drawn her to sculpture in the first place. She'd been trying to write. Getting tangled up in how to deal with time. Then she thought: a sculpture could just stand there. The seasons could pass around it. The light could move around it. You just did.

title: TECHNOLOGY/TRANSFORMATION: WONDER WOMAN
transcript: She keeps spinning. Diana Prince spins, there's a flash of light, and out comes Wonder Woman. Lynda Carter. Boots, bracelets, hair somehow perfect. Then it happens again. And again. By the third time, it's funny. After a few more, it starts to feel a little off. In 1978, Dara Birnbaum gets hold of footage from the Wonder Woman television show and starts chopping. The plot goes. The villain goes. Most of the heroics go. What stays is the thing everybody was waiting for anyway. Spin. Explosion. Superhero. Diana Prince disappears. Wonder Woman shows up. And before she can enjoy it, somebody needs something. Go stop this. Go rescue him. Go save the world. She barely gets the bracelets on before the power gets assigned a job. So Birnbaum yanks her back to the beginning. Spin. Explosion. Superhero. Again. Now you start noticing what a weird little deal television is offering. A flash of light. A new outfit. A perfect body. Done. That's how a woman becomes powerful. It has to look good, happen fast, and be ready for the next episode. Birnbaum repeats the trick until the trick starts looking like a trap. Is Diana controlling the transformation, or is the transformation controlling her? Television in 1978 only goes one way. Into your house. You don't answer it. Video art already existed. Artists had been pointing cameras at themselves for years. But you definitely don't steal television's pictures, cut them up, and send them back. Birnbaum did. Friends inside the industry got her the footage. Birnbaum didn't own a VCR. She cut it on an industrial editing deck. Then she showed the finished video, not in a museum, but in the storefront window of a hair salon in SoHo. A room full of people changing their hair, watching a woman who can't stop changing.

title: DEC. 17, 1979
transcript: DEC.17.1979. That's it. That's the painting. On Kawara had one rule for this series, which he began on January 4, 1966: finish the painting before midnight, or destroy it. Not set it aside. Not come back tomorrow. Destroy it. The date had to be earned on the day it names, or it ceased to exist. He painted this one, put it in a cardboard box, and lined the box with that day's newspaper. Which is such a precise move. He didn't put the news on the painting. He put it underneath. History sitting just below the surface. Not buried. Just held separately. He gave almost no interviews. Refused public photography for decades. And yet for nearly half a century, he left a daily record of his own existence, date by date, city by city. One of the most private artists of the twentieth century made one of the most meticulous autobiographies in the history of art. Not minimalism. Documentation. There's a difference. He also sent telegrams to friends. Just: I AM STILL ALIVE. That was the whole message. The bar was low. He cleared it. Some days, that is the full achievement. And you do not need to decorate it. The last date painting was made in 2013. Then the series stops. No finale. No curtain speech. You go looking for what comes after DEC.17.1979, after all of them, and eventually you run out of paintings. The silence on the other side of the last one is part of the work. So, what did you do on December 17, 1979? On Kawara painted this.

title: THE SLEEPERS (LES DORMEURS)
transcript: Sophie Calle doesn't know what to do with her day. So, she follows somebody who's already having one. Think about that for a second. She's back in Paris after seven years away. No job. No friends left. She picks a stranger in the street and goes wherever they go. Takes photographs. Writes things down. They have somewhere to be. Now she does too. She isn't calling this art yet. It's just something to do. Then a friend who's been working all night asks if she can sleep in Calle's bed. You know, a reasonable request. But Calle takes it quite a bit further. She thinks it would be fun to have somebody in the bed all the time. One person gets up, another gets in. Eight-hour shifts. Keep it going for eight days. So she starts asking people. Friends. Strangers. Bakers, who sleep during the day anyway. A babysitter from an agency. Imagine getting that booking. This is The Sleepers. Paris, 1979. She feeds them, photographs them every hour, writes down what happens. There's a tape recorder. And a questionnaire. She says she's afraid of having strangers in her bed. Also afraid of the silence. She's invited them. She's set the hours. Now she needs help getting through the conversation. One visitor even falls asleep during the questions. When somebody doesn't turn up, her mother fills in. Shows up at noon. Asks for a whiskey. Goes to sleep. At four-thirty, Calle wakes her with champagne. Guess you could say her mother is having a fairly good shift. One of the women she asks at the market happens to be married to an art critic. She goes home and tells him what she's been doing. He asks to see the pictures. The project ends up in an exhibition. That's how Calle says she became an artist. First, though, the critic asks her something. Is this art? She says it could be.

title: MEETING
transcript: To make somewhere this quiet, James Turrell needed a jackhammer. He'd been invited to make a work here, in this old public school in Queens. And he wanted an opening in the roof. Alanna Heiss ran the place. She told him the concrete was probably six to nine inches thick. The building had been designed to carry extra floors above it. Turns out it was four and a half feet. So he had a compressor craned onto the roof and jackhammered his way through. Now you get to sit underneath it. So, look up. That's the actual sky. Whatever's happening over Queens, whether you showed up or not. Around sunset, hidden lights wash the walls in changing colors. When the white walls glow warm orange, the blue up there gets stronger. Change the light in the room, and the same patch of sky looks different. From down here, the edge looks almost impossibly thin. The sky can go flat. Like a panel fitted into the ceiling. All that distance, close enough to touch. This is called Meeting. Turrell grew up Quaker, going to meetings where people sat together in silence. His grandmother told him they were going inside to "greet the light". He also remembers sitting in those meetings, thinking about a car. A '57 Ford. The one that retracted a metal roof back into the trunk. And imagining the meetinghouse could do that. The roof coming off.

title: UNTITLED
transcript: Start with the kid in the hospital bed. 1968. Brooklyn. Jean-Michel Basquiat is seven, playing ball in the street, when a car hits him. Broken arm. Internal injuries. His spleen has to come out. His mother Matilde brings him something to read while he recovers. Gray's Anatomy. The medical book. Muscles with the skin off. Bones with their names printed beside them. The book sticks. Thirteen years later, Basquiat is twenty, making this in oilstick on paper. It looks like it arrived all at once. Three figures stare out, weapons at their sides. Halos over two of them. A crown on the third. Around them, stars, waves, a sun, marks that look half prehistoric, half subway. And in the middle, two animals. One feral, teeth out. The other stripped to a skeleton, ribs showing, and somehow still moving. That's the trick with Basquiat. What looks raw is loaded. Anatomy. Black history. Jazz. Egyptian signs. Street language. Crowns. Nothing kept in its proper department. So sure, the skeleton can mean death. Skeletons usually get stuck with that job. But it also looks like Gray's Anatomy got loose. The book from the hospital bed, thirteen years later, running through the middle of the page. The body with the cover pulled off. The frame underneath. And in these same years, Basquiat was playing in a downtown noise band. The Mudd Club. No album. Barely songs. The band had another name first. Basquiat gave it the one that stuck. He called it Gray.

title: DAVID WOJNAROWICZ
transcript: So, look at the cigarette. It's in his mouth. Two fingers up, holding it there. It's lit. One eye catches the light. The other almost disappears. That's David Wojnarowicz. Peter Hujar took the photograph. Peter was twenty years older. He'd been taking pictures of everybody in the downtown scene for years, ya know, artists, writers, drag performers. Andy Warhol filmed him four times. Called him the boy that never blinked. That's how he worked, too. He'd sit you down and wait. Wait for the face you put on for people to slip. Then he took the picture. His friend Stephen Koch said your portrait was always unmistakably you. But only because it was also unmistakably his. Anyway, Peter and David met at a gay bar in the East Village. They were lovers for a little while. Then that ended, and they stayed close. Peter told him he ought to paint. David had never painted before. So he did. Years later, David said, "Everything I made, I made for Peter." Six years after this picture, Peter's in the hospital with AIDS. David's there a lot. When Peter dies, David asks everyone else to leave the room. He has a camera with him. He photographs Peter's face. His hands. His feet. Peter took this one. David took those. At the funeral, Fran Lebowitz said Peter had hung up on every important photography dealer in the Western world. He said once, "When people talk about me, I want them to be whispering." Outside downtown, while he was alive, his pictures mostly went unnoticed. The younger artists noticed. Nan Goldin. And this guy. Everybody else took a while. David turned into one of the loudest artists of the AIDS years. Five years after Peter, he died of AIDS too. And this photograph? David gave it to the museum.

title: GOVERNMENT APPROVED HOME FALLOUT SHELTER SNACK BAR
transcript: Okay so, in 1980, the federal government put out instructions for turning your basement rec-room into a fallout shelter. There's a snack bar in it. Actual FEMA pamphlet. So in '83, Michael Smith built the thing. Smith and a set designer named Alan Herman. They put it in a gallery in New York. Wood paneling. Linoleum. Easy chair. Records. Barrels of survival crackers. Liquor bottles. Basically, the basement at the end of the world. And the bar has a canopy on hinges. Fold it down, pile concrete blocks on top, and now it's a radiation shield. That part's straight out of the pamphlet. Smith even had a word for the menu. Cuisine. Because nuclear war, he said, is this great democratizing event. Rich guy, poor guy, everybody ends up in the same basement eating the same crackers. So, Smith had been playing this character named Mike since the late seventies. Mike started out as Blandman. A guy basically built to be bland. Mike follows instructions. Mike believes the brochure. And this time, the brochure was real. Oh, and there's one more thing down there. An arcade game. Working joystick. Coin slot. It's called Mike Builds a Shelter. Smith made it with a graphics designer and a teenager who coded the whole thing on a Commodore 64. You play Mike. You put your coin in and the air-raid sirens start. Little 8-bit Mike, carrying three concrete blocks down the stairs before the big one drops. And the game is programmed so nobody can win. Every game ends the same way. Manhattan gets nuked. Then the theme from Dr. Strangelove starts playing.

title: TEARS
transcript: It's small. About the size of a shoebox. A wooden scaffold, a leather bundle on top, words inscribed on the base. Kay WalkingStick made it in 1990. She called it Tears. Walk closer. Read the words. We were twenty million. Now we are two million. The year matters. 1990. America is about to throw itself a five-hundred-year party. The Columbus quincentennial. A whole national celebration of the moment a European guy arrived and started a chain reaction that killed ninety percent of the people who already lived here. WalkingStick is Cherokee. While the country builds parade floats, she builds this. The form is a funerary scaffold. Plains tradition. You lay the body on a raised platform, burn it. The body returns to the earth and rises into the sky at the same time. Two motions at once. Going down. Going up. Memorial sculpture usually picks one. She picks both. Look at the bundle. It's a body. Wrapped in deer hide and cow hide and one piece of leather from a shirt she made for her first husband, who died young. National grief and personal grief, same shoebox, same little fire. You read this close. Quiet. Bent over a little. Which is, probably, the only way to read it at all.

title: DEODORIZED CENTRAL MASS WITH SATELLITES
transcript: You get the smell first. Pine. The industrial kind. The kind that means somebody has cleaned something. Then you look up, and for a second it's actually kind of beautiful. Big fuzzy balls hanging from the ceiling on wires you can hardly see. Blue. Green. Yellow. Planets. That's where your brain goes. Somebody put a solar system in a white room. And these shiny pointed things down both walls. Like pieces off a very expensive car. Kelley called it Deodorized Central Mass with Satellites. The satellites are obvious. The deodorized part is waiting on the walls. Get closer. Stuffed animals. Hundreds of them, sewn into balls. Sorted by color, like laundry. And every one is facing inward. No eyes. No little noses. Nothing in there to make eye contact with. Kelley did that on purpose. He didn't want them pulling sentiment out of you. He'd been working with stuffed animals since 1987. Thrift stores, yard sales. The places objects go after they've been demoted from loved to tolerated to disposable. He thought he was making work about commodity culture. The things we buy to stand in for love. Nobody heard that. They saw the matted fur and the stains and went straight to childhood trauma. Somebody slept with this thing. Cried into it. Carried it through the worst years of being small. Then one day, gone. And they looked at the man sewing them together and decided something terrible must have happened to him. Kelley said he was stunned. Then he did the strangest possible thing. He went with it. If everybody believed buried abuse was hiding underneath the work, fine. He took their diagnosis and started working with that. Repressed memories. Buried trauma. America digging through the child to explain the adult. This one stretches from 1991 to 1999, right through the middle of all that. Now look at the ten shiny shapes on the walls. Kelley called them deodorizers. Every few minutes, pssshhht. Pine. The animals bring in everything messy. Dirt. Memory. Shame. Love. The tasteful modern objects keep trying to clean it up. Forever. Read MoMA's list of materials. Plush toys. Wood. Wire. Styrofoam. Rope. Pulleys. Car paint. And disinfectant.

title: PARADOX OF PRAXIS 1 (SOMETIMES MAKING SOMETHING LEADS TO NOTHING)
transcript: Alright, here's the plan, in full. Get a block of ice. A big one. Mexico City. 1997. Now push it through the streets. No cart. No rope. Start with your hands. Keep going until there's nothing left to push. Francis Alÿs did this for more than nine hours. Nine hours. That's not a gesture. That's a shift. Somewhere in the middle it stops being impressive and starts being a question. He announced the answer in advance. It's the title. Paradox of Praxis 1: Sometimes Making Something Leads to Nothing. At first, the ice is heavy. It fights him. People have to step around this man shoving a perfect white block through traffic. Then, hour by hour, the job gets easier. Exactly as fast as the point of it disappears. Soon he can push it with one hand. Then kick it with his foot. Near the end, the block is the size of an ice cube. Then it's a wet spot. Then Mexico City just keeps being Mexico City. Alÿs had moved there about a decade earlier. An architect who stopped building things. A lot of his work runs on this. Enormous effort, tiny result. Which, depending on the week you're having, is either absurd or extremely familiar. He wasn't mocking it. He was rehearsing it. On purpose. In public. Nine hours of pushing. The video runs five minutes.

title: ŁÓDŹ, OCTOBER 1, 2004
transcript: Alright, start with the cloth. White, little blue squares. Hanging off the machine, piled in neat folds below. Spotless by the yard. OK, now look at the room. Peeling paint. Crumbling brick. A bare tube light. Plastic thrown over the machine. This is a fabric factory in Poland. The place looks like it’s falling apart. But that cloth has no idea. The artist is Christopher Williams. American. Grew up in Los Angeles. He’s part of a big art show in Poland, and they’re using old factory buildings to show the work. Alright, so now think about what a good catalog picture can sell you. A few yards of cloth, sure. But also a clean kitchen. Fresh curtains. A little feeling that your life could be nicer. So… a lot can ride on some blue squares. Williams works with the people who make those pictures. Photographers. Models. People who build sets and get the lights right. He runs the job like a director making a movie. His father worked in special effects in Hollywood. He grew up around people whose whole job was making fake stuff look real. He’s like the magician’s kid who watched the cape get ironed. Anyway, so there are two jobs to think about here. Making the cloth. And making you want it. Maybe that’s the trick. He uses that second job to get you looking at the first. Look at what he leaves in the picture. The wall. The tube light. The plastic sheet. You could crop all that out and have a nice picture of some fabric. But he gives you the place it came from, too. Then photographs the whole mess like it’s for sale.

title: WALL DRAWING #1144, BROKEN BANDS OF COLOR IN FOUR DIRECTIONS
transcript: A man walks into a brand-new gallery carrying a pencil. That's it. No canvas. No crate coming in behind him. He walks up to a bare white wall and starts drawing directly on the building. October 1968. Prince Street, before SoHo was really SoHo. The gallery's first show. The whole thing is a benefit. The money goes to a committee trying to end the war in Vietnam. And on the price list, every other artwork has a number. Sol LeWitt's says: by the hour. Which is, uh, a pretty strange way to sell a drawing. You're paying a man with a pencil to make an idea show up. That first drawing is gone. And, okay, this one can go the same way. Thirty-seven feet of color. Broken bands heading off in four directions. Bright. Orderly. Almost stupidly cheerful. LeWitt didn't draw it. He wrote down the decisions. Colors. Directions. What goes where. Then other people climbed the ladders and made it happen. Instructions go in. Something like stained glass comes out. And when the museum is finished with it, they can just paint the whole thing white. No storage crate. Just a roller. Gone. And, somehow, MoMA still owns the artwork. Because the wall is only where the work is visiting. The plan survives. Take it to another wall and, you know, the whole thing comes back. Different wall. Different hands. Same work. That was the trick. LeWitt kept removing things people thought an artist had to do. Touch the work. Be in the room. Eventually, be alive. LeWitt died in 2007. The next year, more than sixty artists and students spent six months covering nearly an acre of wall in Massachusetts with a hundred and five of his drawings. He wasn't there.

title: WARM BROAD GLOW
transcript: Two words in neon, lowercase. negro sunshine. And the light is doing something wrong. The letters are dark. Ligon had the front of every tube painted with Plasti Dip, an industrial rubber coating. Black, over the glass. The glow can’t come through the words. It leaks out from behind them. A halo around a blackout. Sixteen feet of it. This is Warm Broad Glow, from 2005. Glenn Ligon’s first neon. He left the cords hanging and the transformer boxes on the floor. He doesn’t hide how the light gets made. But the words aren’t his. Gertrude Stein wrote them in 1909, in a book called Three Lives. She’s describing a Black woman named Rose. “Rose laughed when she was happy, but she had not the wide, abandoned laughter that makes the warm broad glow of negro sunshine.” Rose doesn’t have that laughter. That’s what the sentence says. And that’s where the phrase starts to turn. It sounds warm. Almost admiring. But is Stein admiring Black laughter? Or turning it into a type, then measuring Rose against it? Ligon takes his title from the pretty half. The half that stings, he puts on the wall. Then there’s the fight inside the words themselves. “Negro” carries blackness. “Sunshine” is all light. Dark and light, forced into the same phrase. The same problem as the neon. And then it gets harder. Chicago, in the thirties. Richard Wright is still a young Black writer. Native Son is years away. He pulls Three Lives off a public-library shelf and opens to “Melanctha.” The prose starts singing in his ear. He hears his grandmother. Then Wright finds an attack on Stein in a labor journal. Tortured prose. Throttling the revolution. So he runs a test. The way Wright told it, he gathers Black stockyard workers in a basement and reads “Melanctha” out loud. They understand every word. They start slapping their thighs. Laughing. Stomping. Interrupting him to talk about the characters. The wide, abandoned laughter Stein said Rose didn’t have. Here it is, coming from Black workers listening to Stein. So what are they hearing? A stereotype? People they recognize? Something Stein caught without fully understanding? Ligon doesn’t pick one. But, nearly a century later, he puts the words on a wall and plugs them in.

title: UNTITLED
transcript: The letter X is the fastest way to say no. One keystroke. Done. Nothing personal. Now here's a canvas covered in them, top to bottom, and half of them falling apart. The how is where the whole thing starts. Wade Guyton opens Microsoft Word, types an X, repeats it, blows it up. Then he sends it through an Epson Stylus Pro 9600, a large-format inkjet built to print clean images on paper. But this is primed linen. Thick, floppy, not supposed to be in there. It drags. It slips. The ink pools. The image doubles. Guyton leaves all of it in. Look at the right side. Clean Xs. Even spacing. They showed up on time and followed the instructions. Now the left. The Xs bunch together, smear, stack on top of themselves. The machine got one simple job and started losing the plot. At first, the Xs feel like a wall of no. But said this many times, by a machine this tired, they stop sounding final. They start sounding like somebody who's said no all day. Now go back to the smears. The pooling. The doubled image. In a painting, a mark like that is supposed to tell you something about the person who made it. How fast the hand moved. How hard it pressed. Where it hesitated. Here, it tells you the wheels rolled through wet ink. The marks look expressive. But nobody expressed them. He takes all the old evidence of the artist's hand and hands it to a printer. Except the printer can't make the same painting twice. The file stays exactly the same. The object doesn't. And then one detail rearranges the whole canvas. It's seven feet tall, almost six feet wide. Too wide for the printer. So Guyton folded the linen in half down the middle and printed each side separately. Same file. Same machine. Two runs. One mostly behaved. One didn't. The printer never saw the whole painting. Neither did Guyton, until he unfolded it.

title: TROPICAL NIGHT
transcript: Two hundred and sixty-eight drawings hanging from paper clips. Each one about the size of a paperback. It looks like somebody took a notebook apart and pinned it to the wall mid-thought. Around 2006, Christopher Cozier, an artist from Trinidad, is traveling constantly. Residencies, biennials, invitations. His studio keeps changing. A hotel room. A friend's place. Wherever he can sit down. So he starts drawing on sheets small enough to pack flat. Nine inches by seven. Then he keeps going for eight years. Meanwhile, the title is running a con on you. Tropical Night. Your brain supplies the beach. Warm breeze. Drink with fruit in it. The Caribbean made for people who have return tickets. The drawings don't cooperate. Little figures. Fences. Notes scribbled over notes. A map keeps showing up. A dime-store rubber stamp, printed wet enough that the latitudes smear. Shapes repeat from sheet to sheet the way worries do. Whatever this tropical night is, nobody's sleeping. And nothing here stays fixed. The drawings hang from clips because Cozier rearranges them every time they're shown. Same pages. Different thought. Now find the grapes. A neat little cluster. They keep turning up, sheet after sheet. Cozier didn't invent them. He took them from the cover of Nelson's West Indian Readers, a British schoolbook first published in 1928 that taught generations of Caribbean children to read. Before they could write their own sentences, somebody had already picked the pictures. Cozier spent eight years filling these pages. Some of it was waiting for him before he was born.

title: HEAD OF JAKE
transcript: It looks like it took about twenty minutes. One stroke for the mouth. A dash for an eye. A ridge of paint where the nose goes. The dark red lines do the drawing. Cheek, jaw, chin. The shoulders are one big cream sweep. Fast enough to still look wet. A head, about life-size. You can nearly count the marks. The date says 2006 to 2007. So where did a year of painting go? Auerbach painted in the same Camden studio most of his life. Went in nearly every day. And the same few people came to him. Same day, same hour, week after week. Some of them for forty years. At the end of a sitting, he'd look at what he had. If it wasn't right, he scraped it off. All of it. Down to the canvas. Next week, same person, start again. The head you're left with is the last one. The one he didn't scrape. The scrapings just piled up around the easel. Now. The sitter. Jake is his son. And when Jake was a kid, they didn't see each other at all. Twelve years. They met again in 1976. Then Jake started coming to the studio. Same day, same hour. He kept that slot for decades. Sat still while his father painted him, scraped him off, and painted him again. A year of those sittings came down to this one head. Almost none of the others survived. The appointment did.

title: COLOMBIA
transcript: Alright. Look. It's just a word. Take it in for a second. Red background. White script. The font you've seen ten thousand times in your life, on a can, on a vending machine, on a sign at every corner store from here to Bogotá. Your brain is already finishing the word for you. Co, co You know how this goes. Then your eye catches up. Oh. Wait. That little stumble, that half-second where your brain says Coca-Cola and your eye says no, it's Colombia, that's the whole thing.
